units.la: QUamvis S. Scriptura sit lucerna pedibus nostris Ps. CXIX. 105. ותורה אור & lex lux Prov. VI. 23. in qua πεφωτισμένοι τῆς ὀφθαλμὸς τῆς διανοίας Eph. 1. 18. liquidissimam primariorum doctrinæ Christianæ capitum fixo aspectu contemplari possunt veritatem: certum tamen est, nec ulla cum dubitatione conjunctum, non quædam tantùm Scripturæ loca noctuarum ad istud λαμπρὸν φάος ἡελίοιο caligantium perversitate, & eorum potissimùm, qui tanti Solis luminibus, tenebrosas objiciendo nubeculas, obstruere non verecundantur, malitiâ fidiculis torqueri, sed & alia splendore suo summa perstringere ingenia, simúlque omne tædium naúseámque abstergere iis qnoque, qui tanquam ἀεῖοι ἐν νεφέλαις ultra communem hominum valentiam sunt perspicaces.
units.tr: Although Holy Scripture is a lamp to our feet (Ps. 119:105) and the law is light [ותורה אור] (Prov. 6:23), in which those who are enlightened in the eyes of the understanding (Eph. 1:18) can contemplate with a steady gaze the clearest truth of the chief doctrines of Christianity, it is nevertheless certain, and beyond any doubt, that not only certain passages of Scripture are tormented by the malice of owls, that is, of those who are dazzled by the bright light of the sun [λαμπρὸν φάος ἡελίοιο], and most of all by those who are not ashamed to block the lights of so great a Sun by throwing little dark clouds before them. Other passages also strike the highest intellects with their brilliance, and at the same time wipe away all weariness and disgust even from those who, as if always among the clouds [ἀεῖοι ἐν νεφέλαις], are keen-sighted beyond the ordinary power of men.

units.la: II. Est exempli loco textus ad ἀναστάσεως τῶν νεκρῶν in Epistolis Paulinis, monente Petro 2 Ep. III. 16. occurrentia meritissimò adscribendus, quem 1. Cor. XV. 29. hunc in modum serae relictum posteritati legimus: Ἐπεὶ τί ποιήσουσιν οἱ βαπτιζόμενοι ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν, εἰ ὅλως νεκροὶ οὐκ ἐγείρονται; τί καὶ βαπτίζονται ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν νεκρῶν; Alioqui (vel praeterea) quid facient ij, qui baptizantur pro mortuis, si omnino mortui non suscitantur? cur ergo baptizantur pro mortuis? Hoc sanè tremenda, quo magnus Doctor gentium præter gravissima, quibus in antecedentibus pro cujusque pondere immoratus est, argumenta mortuorum in vitam reversionem contra eos, qui in Corinthiorum Ecclesia occultos ad eam diruendam suffoderunt cuniculos, constabilire voluit; tum veteres, tum recentiores Scripturæ Tractatores ita habuit exercitos, ut in ejus enucleatione haud mediocriter desudando, mirabili judiciorum discrepantiâ, propriam plerique dicere sententiam, quàm alienæ suffragium commodare præoptârint, & quò diutius considerârunt, eò avidius scire desiderârint, ad quem morem & ritum Apostolus digitum indendat.
units.tr: II. As an example, the text on the resurrection of the dead in the Pauline Epistles deserves to be cited, as Peter warns (2 Pet. 3:16). We read it, left late to posterity, in 1 Cor. 15:29: Otherwise, what will they do who are baptized for the dead, if the dead do not rise at all? Why then are they baptized for the dead? [Ἐπεὶ τί ποιήσουσιν οἱ βαπτιζόμενοι ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν, εἰ ὅλως νεκροὶ οὐκ ἐγείρονται; τί καὶ βαπτίζονται ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν νεκρῶν;] Indeed, this is a fearsome passage, in which the great Teacher of the Gentiles, besides the most weighty arguments he had dwelt on in the preceding verses, according to the weight of each, wished to establish the return of the dead to life against those who had dug secret tunnels to undermine the Church at Corinth. Both ancient and more recent interpreters of Scripture have so wrestled with it that, labouring hard over its explanation, and with a remarkable disagreement of judgements, most have preferred to state their own opinion rather than lend support to another's. The longer they considered it, the more eagerly they wished to know what custom and rite the Apostle is pointing to.

units.la: III. Etsi autem in hoc ἄπορον τῆς θείας γραφῆς inquirere pro more habeant γνήσιοι Μωσέως ἑρμηνευταὶ καὶ ἱεροφάνται, queis doctior orbis submissis defert fascibus imperium: Quia tamen superiorum excellen-
units.tr: III. However, although the genuine interpreters and expositors of Moses [γνήσιοι Μωσέως ἑρμηνευταὶ καὶ ἱεροφάνται], to whom the more learned world submits and yields its rods of rule, are accustomed to inquire into this difficulty of divine Scripture [ἄπορον τῆς θείας γραφῆς], yet because the excellence of those above

units.la: tiam inferiorum restinguere studia & infringere audentiam minime oportet, inque hujusmodi caligine & acutioribus & hebetioribus ingeniis eadem pene fors est, non erit περιεργία ἀχρήστως πεάγματα, neque verebor paulò confidentius dissonas multiplicesque variorum de hoc loco opiniones, Θεῦ χειραγωγῶν, invicem collidere & αὐτόματα penficulare, falsas & praeposteritatem habentes rejicere, pias & probabiles inspicere, τῶ ἀρέσκοντι denique elicere, quae si minus videbitur consentanea, sat erit Aristarchis medicam manum offerendi atque adeo meliora suggerendi occasionem obtulisse: sin forte ex ejusmodi conflictatione pulchra quaedam veritatis scintilla dissiliet, bene laetae eritis res.
units.tr: should by no means quench the zeal of those below, nor break their boldness, and since in such darkness the same chance falls to sharper and duller minds alike, it will not be idle busybodying with useless matters [περιεργία ἀχρήστως πράγματα] if I venture, somewhat more boldly, to set against one another the discordant and manifold opinions of various writers on this passage, with God as guide [Θεοῦ χειραγωγοῦντος], and to weigh them for myself. I will reject those that are false and absurd, examine those that are pious and probable, and finally draw out what pleases [τῷ ἀρέσκοντι]. If some of these seem out of keeping, it will be enough to have offered the physician's hand to the critics of Aristarchus and to have given them the occasion to suggest better things. But if from such a conflict some fine spark of truth should leap out, your affairs will go very happily.

units.la: IV. Ut vero ἐκ τῶν ἀπόρων πρὸν εὑρίσκειν proclivius fit, diversas interpretationes juxta tres potiores verbi βαπτίζειν significationes ordine examinare pretium fuerit operae. Βαπτίζειν namque; quod ἐκ τῆς βάπτειν mergere, inficere profluxit, & κυρολεκτως intingi, immergi, denotat; per Metaphoram amarissimis gravissimarum afflictionum undis submergi Matth.XX.22. Marc.X.38. Luc.XII.50. per Synecdochen & καὶ ἐξαίρετον mystica lympha perfundi, h.e. Sacramenti immatriculationis in Ecclesiam tessera, tanquam Christiani tinctura, notari; per Metonymiam finis in genere lavari vel ablui significat. Harum significationum quamlibet varij variè loco proposito adaptare moliuntur.
units.tr: IV. So that finding out from difficulties [ἐκ τῶν ἀπόρων] may be easier, it will be worth the effort to examine in order the different interpretations according to the three chief meanings of the word baptizein. For βαπτίζειν, which comes from βάπτειν, to dip or steep, properly denotes to be dipped or immersed. By metaphor, it means to be submerged in the bitter waves of most grievous afflictions (Matt. 20:22; Mark 10:38; Luke 12:50). By synecdoche and eminently, it means to be sprinkled with mystical water, that is, to be marked with the token of the sacrament of enrolment in the Church, as a Christian is dyed. By metonymy of the end, it signifies in general to be washed or cleansed. Various writers try to fit each of these meanings to the passage in various ways.

units.la: V. Et Metaphorica quidem ad Pontificis Rom. gnathonum ac cineriorum est salivam, qui in dicto hoc Paulino se reperisse putant non quod pueri in faba: Ex eo enim vivorum pro mortuis suffragia, unde currente rota Purgatorij exeat urceus, exterebrare manibus pedibusque nituntur. Est igitur expositio vera & germana (sic magistraliter argutatur primarius ille Thaidis Romanae procus Bellarminus disp. T.II.l.1. de Purg.c.6. p.396.) quod Apostolus loquatur de baptismo lacrymarum & poenitentia, qui suscipitur orando, jejunando, eleemosynas faciendo, &c. Et sensus sit: Quid facient qui baptizantur pro mortuis, si mortui non resurgent? id est, quid facient qui orant, jejunant, gemunt, affligunt se pro mortuis, si mortui non resurgunt? Ei praeter alios haud ita multos adhinnit Jesuita Fr. Costerus Enchir. controv.c.16.p.m.498. cui baptizari est affligi orationibus, jejuniis, & id genus aliis modis. En Chrysippeum acumen! De istis Synagogae Rom. Scipionibus excidit mihi exclamare, sicut de Scipione Nasica Cato major & de Chrysippo veteres ex Homero dicere consueverunt: Οἱ μὲν πεπνυμένοι, λοιπὸὶ σκιαὶ ἀίσσουσιν: Hi soli sapiunt, alii velut umbra feruntur, cum nemo ante ipsos tam argutus fuerit & acutus, qui hoc in loco Purgatorium viderit aut suffragia.
units.tr: V. The metaphorical interpretation belongs to the flatterers and ash-men of the Roman Pontiff, who think they have found in this Pauline saying something not to be sought in the way children look for the bean in a cake. For they strive with hands and feet to wrest from it the intercessions of the living for the dead, so that when the wheel of Purgatory turns, the jug comes out. The interpretation is therefore true and genuine (so the chief champion of the Roman Thais, Bellarmine, argues in his masterly fashion, Disp. T. II, l. 1, de Purg. c. 6, p. 396), that the Apostle is speaking of the baptism of tears and of repentance, which is undertaken by praying, fasting, giving alms, and so on. And the sense is: What will they do who are baptized for the dead, if the dead do not rise? That is, what will those do who pray, fast, groan, and afflict themselves for the dead, if the dead do not rise? Besides others, not very many, the Jesuit Fr. Costerus also neighs in agreement (Enchir. controv. c. 16, p. 498), for whom to be baptized is to be afflicted with prayers, fasts, and other such means. Behold the Chrysippean subtlety! Concerning these Scipios of the Roman synagogue, I cannot help crying out what the ancients were accustomed to say of Scipio Nasica, Cato the Elder, and Chrysippus, borrowing from Homer: The wise alone have sense; the rest flit about like shadows [Οἱ μὲν πεπνυμένοι, λοιποὶ σκιαὶ ἀίσσουσιν]. For before them no one has been so keen and sharp as to have seen Purgatory or intercessions in this passage.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Veruntamen, si fas rem fari, isthaec loci evolutio, an involutio, talis est, ut si posito certamine enarrationibus vitiosis aliqua corona proponeretur, sola hoc nomine contra omnes coronanda videri queat. Etenim 1. alienam verbo baptizari, cujus nec in Scriptura, nec apud Patres extat exemplum, affingit significationem. In Scriptura quidem figurata haec locutio βαπτίζεσθαι βάπτισμα afflictiones non quaslibet, sed vehementes, easque non electitias aut ultro sumtas, sed forinsecus illatas aut irruentes designat. Sicut enim non est, qui baptizer semetipsum baptismo fluminis aut flaminis, sed illo Ecclesiae minister per aquae elementi aspectabilis asperionem, hoc Christus ipse per gratiam donorum S. Spiritus effusionem: ita nec baptismo sanguinis seu tribulationum dicuntur baptizari, qui sua sponte afflictant se ipsos, sed qui calamitates a Deo immissas moderate ferunt. Patres vero, quibus eandem fere cum baptismo Sacramentali tribuunt virtutem, iis quoque baptismi vocem applicant. Ita martyrium ipsis est baptisma virtutis, non afflictionis vel passionis, respectu, quod eo in Catechumenis ante baptismum ad martyrium abrepris baptismus suppleatur, & iisdem tantum commodet, quantum baptismus. Eodem plane modo lachrymas & poenitentiam in iis, qui ἀβαπτίστοι decesserunt, cum lacrymis tamen seriam egerunt poenitentiam, baptismi vicem, ratione valoris sustinere censuerunt. Interim similitudini operationis addiderunt & fundamenti loco posuerunt convenientiam quandam in ablutione, quod quemadmodum in fluminis baptismo aqua perfundimur, sic martyr sanguine suo, poenitens lacrymis suis irrigetur. Quid v. haec ad orationes, eleemosynas, jejunia, afflictiones pro mortuis? 2. Etiamsi largiremur eis hanc interpretationem (ita Forbesius Instruct. Hist. Theol. I. 13, c. 12. §. 30.) non assequerentur quod intendunt. Nam Apostolus hinc sumit argumentum pro corporum resurrectione: De animarum autem separatarum ex aliquibus poenis liberatione ante diem resurrectionis corporum nihil invenitur apud Apostolum. Certe Metaphoricus ille activae afflictionis baptismus a Papistis suscipitur non ut defunctorum corpora resurgant, sed ut animulae in poenalibus Purgatorii claustris detentae remissionem peccatorum & missionem a cruciatu ante pancriticum resurrectionis diem impetrent.
units.tr: Yet, if I may speak plainly, this unfolding (or rather, unrolling) of the passage is such that, were a contest held in which the prize went to whoever made the most faulty interpretations, it could seem that this crown should go to it alone, against all rivals. For, first, it attaches to the word baptizari a meaning that does not belong to it, and for which there is no example either in Scripture or among the Fathers. In Scripture, the figurative expression to be baptized, a baptism [βαπτίζεσθαι βάπτισμα] denotes afflictions: not just any afflictions, but severe ones, and not those chosen or undertaken of one's own accord, but those inflicted from outside or breaking in upon us. For just as no one baptizes himself with water or with the Spirit, but the minister of the Church baptizes with the sprinkling of the visible element of water, and Christ himself baptizes by pouring out the gifts of the Holy Spirit by grace, so too those are not said to be baptized with the baptism of blood or of tribulations who afflict themselves of their own will, but those who bear calamities sent by God with moderation. The Fathers, however, who ascribe to martyrdom almost the same power as to sacramental baptism, apply the name of baptism to it as well. Thus martyrdom is for them a baptism of virtue, not of affliction or suffering, so that the baptism of those catechumens who are dragged off to martyrdom before baptism is supplied by it, and it benefits them just as much as baptism does. In exactly the same way, they judged that tears and repentance take the place of baptism, as regards its effect, in those who died unbaptized [ἀβαπτίστοι], though they performed serious repentance with tears. At the same time, they added a likeness of operation and took as their foundation a certain resemblance in washing: just as we are drenched with water in river baptism, so the martyr is bathed in his own blood and the penitent in his own tears. But what do these things have to do with prayers, almsgivings, fasts and afflictions for the dead? Second, even if we granted them this interpretation (so Forbesius, Instruct. Hist. Theol. I. 13, c. 12, §. 30), they would not reach what they aim at. For the Apostle draws from this an argument for the resurrection of bodies; but nothing is found in the Apostle about the liberation of separated souls from certain penalties before the day of the resurrection of bodies. Surely that metaphorical baptism of active affliction is taken up by the Papists not so that the bodies of the dead may rise, but so that the little souls held in the penal cloisters of Purgatory may obtain forgiveness of sins and release from torment before the day of the resurrection, the great judgment.

units.la: 3. Christianos, dum viridior aetas Ecclesiae virginitatem tueretur, orâsse, jejunâsse, eleemosynas erogâsse, eo fine & consilio, ut vitâ functorum animabus liberationem ex Igne quodam Purgatorio accelerarent, falsâ ratione receptum est. Illud enim fabulosum πῦρ καθαρτήριον (quod post Apostolorum decessum in scriptis Apocryphis, ex Judaismi, Poetarum ac Philosophorum Gentilium seminibus gravidi, reliquiis, sub nomine Jacobi, Andreae, & Hermae vulgatis, docente Excell. Dn. Praesìde qq. Theol. de fide decret. Concil. Trid. p. 264. primò quidem conceptum; lapsis deinde temporibus, praesertim florente Augustino, qui cum coaetaneis dubitanter admodum & quasi problematicè de eo disseruit, enatum; demum saeculo VI. sub Gregorio M. fovẽntibus superstitionem mortuorum spectris, roboratum; tum porrò Sacrificulorum φιλαργυρία amplificatum; tandemque pro fidei Papisticae articulo obtrusum est) Ecclesiae nascenti fundit-us ignotum fuisse notius est, quàm ut à me commemorandum probandumque videatur.
units.tr: Third, the notion that Christians, while the younger age of the Church kept its virginity, prayed, fasted and gave alms for the purpose and intention of hastening the release of the departed from a certain purgatorial fire, was received on a false basis. That fable of a purgatorial fire [πῦρ καθαρτήριον], which after the death of the Apostles was first conceived, pregnant with the seeds of Judaism, of the poets and of the Gentile philosophers, in the remnants of apocryphal writings spread under the names of James, Andrew and Hermas (as the most distinguished Lord President teaches in his Theological Questions on the Faith of the Decrees of the Council of Trent, p. 264); then, as time passed, especially under the flourishing Augustine, who discussed it with his contemporaries quite hesitantly and as a matter of debate, it grew up; finally, in the sixth century under Gregory the Great, when those who nurtured the superstition of the dead strengthened it with apparitions of spirits; then the love of money [φιλαργυρία] of the priests magnified it further; and at last it was thrust upon us as an article of Papist faith. That this was utterly unknown to the newborn Church is too well known to need my mentioning or proving it.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Neque est, quòd hoc argumentum, quo praeter alia quaedam indigna plane, quae in campum eliciantur, causam desperatam statuminare satagit Jesuitarum os, pulverem cuiquam ob oculos spargat: ipsam nempe Purgatorij poenam à Scriptura & Patribus vocari baptisma, ut Matth. III. 11, baptizabit vos Spiritu S. & igne: adeoque qui se pro mortuis affligunt oratione, jejunio, fletu, &c. suscipere in se partem baptismi illius ignei. Etenim 1. si in allegato Matthaei loco, in quo ἡφαιστεῖον δεσμὸν se invenisse confidit Bellarminus, sub ignis vocabulo delitescit Purgatorium, erit sanè illud beneficium, non supplicium, & pertinebit ad omnes, qui S. Spiritu baptizantur: quae nugae Siculis gerris vaniores vel alicui Heraclito risum ἄσβεστον excuterent. 2. Genuinus loci sensus hic est: Christus vos baptizabit Spiritu igneo, in regeneratione ignis officium naturámque habente. Res enim una saepe numero conjunctione interveniente diducitur & duabus vocibus explicatur non solùm apud profanos autores, ut cùm Virgil. pateris, inquit, libamus & auro, pro, aureis pateris, chalybem frenósque momordit, h.e. chalybea fraena: Sed in ipsis etiam divinorum librorum monumentis, ut Matth. XVII. 21. Act. XIV. 13. Rom. I. 5. Ita Ioh. III. 5, renasciex aquæ & Spi& Spiritu nihil est aliud, quàm renasci ex aqua spirituali, qnæ S. Spiritus est, Esaj. XLIV. 3. Joh. VII. 38. 39. sive è Spiritu, qui, ut loquitur πνευμάτεγας Calvinus Instit. c. 17. §. 45. purgando & irrigando fideles animas vice aquæ fungitur. Comparili ratione Matth. III. 11. ἐνδίκα δυοῖν exprimitur, estque nomen ignis vice appositi: transfertur autem ad Spiritum S. tum quia est instar ignis propter penetrationem virtutis suæ, dum sordes animarum nostrarum purgat, sicut ignis aurum à scoriis excoquit, nos etiam ad amorem Dei & proximi accendit: tum quia Christus Apostolos baptizaturus erat miraculosa donorum S. Spiritûs sub specie ignis seu ignearum linguarum effusione ad indicandam vim ejus & efficacem in animis credentium operationem: huc pertinet Act. I. s. 3. Antiqui Ecclesiæ Doctores, Lactant. Ambros. Hieron. alij, Origenem, malum dogmatistam, secuti, sinxerunt, Sanctos juxta omnes ac impios, nullu ne B. Virgine, Martyribus & Apostolis quidem exceptis, in fine seculi ejusmodi ignem transituros, quali olim ardebunt omnes impii, ut infit Celeb. D. Præses loc. th. 6. cit. vid. Lactant. divin. Instit. l. 7. c. 21. Hunc ignem probatorium aliqui ex nominatis Patribus baptismum ignis nuncupârunt. At veròPurgatorium Papisticum, elapsarum è corporibus humanis animarum, criminum venialium labe contaminatarum, conventiculum, à sana & præstigiis Antichristi nondum fascinata antiquitate baptisma esse appellatum, hoc probet Bellarminus, ἐχ ἀρίξας νικᾶσω. Cùm itaque, qui Purgatoriam incudem tanquam Cyclopes in antri sinuosi faucibus certatim tundunt, interpretationes nonnihil perplexas ac titubantes tanquam columnas tremulas suæ sententiæ suffulciant, & ipsa de Metaphorico voluntariæ afflictionis baptismo glossa, quocunque modo illis libeat διαλεπτολογίας, sit, ei convellendæ diutius immorari supervacaneum fuerit.
units.tr: Nor is there reason why this argument, along with certain other utterly unworthy points that are dragged onto the field, which the Jesuits' mouth labours to prop up a cause they have already given up for lost, should throw dust in anyone's eyes: namely, that the very penalty of Purgatory is called a baptism by Scripture and the Fathers, as in Matthew 3:11, "He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire", and therefore those who afflict themselves for the dead by prayer, fasting, weeping, etc., undertake a share in that fiery baptism. For, first, if in the cited passage of Matthew, in which Bellarmine confidently believes he has found a [ἡφαιστεῖον δεσμόν] fiery bond, Purgatory lies hidden under the word fire, then that will certainly be a benefit, not a punishment, and it will apply to all who are baptized with the Holy Spirit. These trifles would make the Sicilian gerrae seem more empty, or would stir up an unquenchable [ἄσβεστον] laughter in any Heraclitus. Second, the genuine sense of the passage is this: Christ will baptize you with fiery Spirit, the Spirit having the office and nature of fire in regeneration. For one thing is often divided, by an intervening conjunction, and explained by two words, not only in profane authors, as when Virgil says "we pour libations from patens and gold", meaning golden patens, and "he bit the bronze and the bridles", that is, the bronze bridles; but also in the very monuments of the divine books, as in Matthew 17:21, Acts 14:13 and Romans 1:5. So John 3:5, to be born again of water and the Spirit, is nothing other than to be born of spiritual water, which is the Holy Spirit (Isaiah 44:3; John 7:38–39), or of the Spirit, who, as Calvin speaks, Institutes c. 17, §. 45, by cleansing and watering faithful souls, takes the place of water. By a similar reasoning, Matthew 3:11 expresses [ἐν δυοῖν] a single thing in two words, and the name of fire is put in apposition as a kind of substitute. It is transferred to the Holy Spirit, first because he is like fire by the penetration of his power, as he cleanses the filth of our souls, just as fire smelts gold from its dross, and also kindles us to the love of God and of our neighbour; and second because Christ was about to baptize the Apostles by the miraculous pouring out of the gifts of the Holy Spirit under the appearance of fire, or of tongues of fire, to indicate his power and his effective operation in the souls of believers. To this belongs Acts 1:5 and 2:3. The ancient doctors of the Church, Lactantius, Ambrose, Jerome and others, following Origen, that bad dogmatist, imagined that all the saints, without exception, not even the Blessed Virgin, the martyrs and the Apostles excepted, would pass through such a fire at the end of the age, as all the impious will then burn, as the same most celebrated Lord President says in the Loci Theologici, 6, cited above; see Lactantius, Divine Institutes, book 7, c. 21. Some of those named Fathers called this testing fire the baptism of fire. But that the Papist Purgatory, a conventicle of souls that have slipped out of human bodies and are stained with the stain of venial sins, was called a baptism by antiquity not yet bewitched by the sound and the deceptions of Antichrist, Bellarmine must prove [ἐκ τῆς ἀρχῆς νικῶ]. Since, then, those who, like Cyclopes at the mouths of a winding cave, vie with one another in hammering out the Purgatorial anvil, prop up their opinion with somewhat perplexed and wavering interpretations, like trembling columns, and since the gloss itself on a metaphorical baptism of voluntary affliction, in whatever way it pleases them to hair-split [διαλεπτολογίας], it would be superfluous to linger long in overturning it.

units.la: VIII. In saniore sententia locati sunt alii prosapiæ Pontificiæ viri, Gagnejus Doctor Sorbonæ, Claud. Guiliaudus, itidem Doctor Parisiensis, apud Corn. à Lapide comm. in Epist. Paul. p. 327. Maldonatus comm. in Matth. XX. 22. & Luc. XII. 50. quibus baptizari pro mortuis idem est ac affligi seu mortem oppetere pro fide & articulo resurrectionis mortuorum. Paria fere cum his facit vir multijugâ eruditione & famâ nominis celeberrimus D. Rivetus, qui verba Apostoli Cathol. Orthod.
units.tr: VIII. Placed in a saner opinion are other men of the Papist stock: Gagnaeus, Doctor of the Sorbonne, and Claude Guillaud, likewise a Doctor of Paris, cited by Cornelius à Lapide, commentary on the Epistles of Paul, p. 327, and Maldonatus, commentary on Matthew 20:22 and Luke 12:50. For them, to be baptized for the dead means the same as to be afflicted, or to meet death, for the faith and the article of the resurrection of the dead. Almost the same as these is Master Rivet, most celebrated for his many-sided learning and the fame of his name, who, rendering the words of the Apostle in his Catholicus Orthodoxus,

units.la: ita πααραφεάζει: Quid agent, qui singulis diebus persecutiones patiuntur ob mortuos, nempe J. Christum adhuc a morte, si qua dicunt vera sunt, detentum? itemque ut mortuorum fidem ac confessionem defendant? denique ut Christi omniumque Sanctorum resurrectionem propugnent? Huc etiam tendit meditatio Fr. Junii, quam in Notis ad Versionem Paraphraseos Syriacæ Tremellianam hisce illigavit verbis: Alioquin, ait Paulus, si Christus non resurrexerit, neque finem assequuntur, neque consilio sapiunt viventes, quicunque adhuc in Ecclesia affliguntur & persequutiones patiuntur credentes in mortem, sepulturam & resurrectionem Christi. Fine, nam quid facturi sunt alioqui, aut quid eis futurum est? Consilio, nam cur patiuntur ista, si none est resurrectio? Non potest esse inanis illorum fides, aut illi adhuc jacere in peccatis suis, h. e. carere redemtione Christi. Est autem baptizari super mortuos, eis qui pro Christo vitam abjecerunt superaddi & contumulari eis. Loquitur ergo Apostolus, Junii arbitratu, de iis, qui ultra vel praeter mortuos, h. e. illos, qui in fide resurrectionis Christi & spe propriae resurrectionis constituti coronam martyrii receperunt, eâdem fide ac spe subnixi sanguinem suum Christo largiri & per martyrum vestigia ambulare non dubitârunt.
units.tr: paraphrases them thus [παραφράζει]: "What will those do who every day suffer persecutions on account of the dead, namely, if Jesus Christ is still held by death, as they say, is it true? And likewise, that they may defend the faith and confession of the dead? Finally, that they may champion the resurrection of Christ and of all the saints?" To this also tends the reflection of Francis Junius, which he tied to these words in his Notes on the Tremellian Version of the Syriac Paraphrase: "Otherwise," says Paul, "if Christ has not risen, they neither reach the end, nor do the living act wisely, all who are still in the Church afflicted and suffering persecutions, believing in the death, burial and resurrection of Christ. For the end: what will they do otherwise, or what will become of them? For the wisdom: why do they suffer these things, if there is no resurrection? Their faith cannot be empty, or they still lie in their sins," that is, lack the redemption of Christ. "But to be baptized over the dead is to add to those who have cast away their lives for Christ, and to be buried with them." So the Apostle speaks, in Junius's judgment, of those who, beyond or apart from the dead, that is, those who, established in faith in the resurrection of Christ and in hope of their own resurrection, received the crown of martyrdom, and, supported by the same faith and hope, did not hesitate to pour out their blood for Christ and to walk in the footsteps of the martyrs.

units.la: IX. Cæterum, licet hæ expositiones nihil quicquam, quod analogiæ fidei contrariâ gradiatur viâ, contineant, possunt tamen ad illas infirmandas in scenam produci rationes, quas explico in hæc verba.
units.tr: IX. Moreover, although these explanations contain nothing that runs counter to the analogy of faith, arguments can still be brought onto the stage to weaken them. I set them out in the following words.

units.la: 1. Duriusculum videtur, ut, qui patiuntur pro fide vel spe resurrectionis mortuorum, ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν baptizari dicantur, cùm ita male stet articulus τῶν, qui vocem indefinitam determinat & restringit: nec vocabulum ἀναστάσεως commodè subintelligi possit, cùm sic potius ὑπὲρ τῆς ἀναστάσεως νεκρῶν dicendum fuisset. Nova quoque est versio particulæ ὑπὲρ per ultra vel praeter, cui Junius favet.
units.tr: 1. It seems rather harsh that those who suffer for the faith or the hope of the resurrection of the dead should be said to be baptized "for the dead" [ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν], since the article τῶν, which determines and restricts the indefinite noun, does not fit well here. Nor can the word ἀναστάσεως [resurrection] reasonably be understood, since it would have been better to say ὑπὲρ τῆς ἀναστάσεως νεκρῶν [for the resurrection of the dead]. The rendering of the particle ὑπὲρ as beyond or apart from is also new, and Junius favours it.

units.la: 2. Si baptismum crucis in argumentum duxisset Apostolus, non in tertia persona dixisset: Quid facient qui baptizantur: sed in prima se ipsum iis adnumerasset, cùm & ipse spei resurrectionis innixus præsentaneis periculis propter Christum quotidie fuerit expositus, uti liquet ex v. 30. Cur etiam nos periclitamur omni momento?
units.tr: 2. If the Apostle had taken baptism of the cross as his argument, he would not have said in the third person, What will those do who are baptized? He would have included himself among them in the first person, since he too, relying on the hope of resurrection, was exposed to present dangers every day for Christ's sake, as is clear from v. 30: Why do we also face danger every hour?

units.la: 3. Non est exploratum & evidens, quod juxta Gagnæi, Guiliandi, & Maldonati explanationem necessariò præsupponitur, quosdam nim. sub tempora Pauli afflictos & gloriosò martymartyrio affectós esse propterea, quòd articulo de resurrectione mortuorum fidem adjunxerint. Si enim ad primam usque originem & q. punctum, unde series seu processus persecutionum erga Christi militiam professos ducitur, penetremus, solum Christi nomen & sanam de eo confessionem, absque ulteriori dogmatum examine, persecutoribus innatum adversus Christo initiatos odium dirissimis supplicis exsaturandi ansam praebuisse comperiemus. Hinc Neronis, qui autor & dedicator damnationis Christianorum extitit, hoc fuisse decretum traditur: Quisquis Christianum se esse confitetur, is tanquam generis humani convictus hostis sine ulteriore sui defensione capite plectitor, ut notant Alsted. Thef. Chronol. tit. 35. p. m. 331. & Stratem. Theat. Hist. exit. 6. p. 324. Huic assertioni non obstat Paulus, qui Act. XXIII. 6. de spe, inquit, & resurrectione mortuorum ego in judicium vocor. Id enim verborum fecit, tum ut iniquos judices suos, Pharisaeos & Sadducaeos, extremè quidem & odiis & dogmatibus disidentes, concordissimè tamen ad extinguendum Evangelii lumen conspirantes, inter se committeret, & à Pharisaeis saltem salutarem extorqueret literam: tum ut ipsis Pharisaeis sublatâ causâ, virtute sc. & resurrectione Christi crucifixi, qui illis erat scandalum 1. Cor. I. 23. tolli quoque causatum, nostram putà resurrectionem, in mentem redigeret.
units.tr: 3. It is not established and evident that, according to the explanation of Gagnaeus, Guilandus and Maldonatus, it must be presupposed that certain men in Paul's time were afflicted and crowned with glorious martyrdom because they had joined faith in the article of the resurrection of the dead. For if we penetrate to the first origin, the point from which the series or course of persecutions against those who professed Christ's warfare is derived, we shall find that the mere name of Christ and a sound confession of him, without any further examination of doctrines, gave persecutors the occasion to satisfy their innate hatred of those initiated into Christ with the most dreadful punishments. Hence it is handed down that this decree came from Nero, who was the author and originator of the condemnation of Christians: Whoever confesses himself a Christian, being convicted as an enemy of the human race, is to be punished with death without any further defence, as Alsted, Thef. Chronol., title 35, p. 331 and Stratemann, Theat. Hist., exit 6, p. 324 note. Paul does not stand against this assertion, for in Act. XXIII. 6 he says: Concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead I am called in question. He said this in order both to set against one another his unjust judges, the Pharisees and Sadducees, who differed most sharply in their hatreds and doctrines yet conspired most harmoniously to extinguish the light of the Gospel, and to draw at least a salutary word from the Pharisees. He also did it so that, the cause being removed, namely the power and resurrection of the crucified Christ, which was a stumbling block to them (1 Cor. I. 23), they might also be brought to mind, as they supposed, of our resurrection.

units.la: X. Seorsim ab aliis sentit nobilissimum Belgarum decus & profundioris doctrinae ὑπερέχον φέγγος Anna Maria à Schurman, quae in Epist. ad Jac. Lydium perscripta locum nostrum refert ad ministros Christi, qui, dum propagandis Ecclesiis perpetuò invigilarent, maximis eâ tempestate persecutionibus & calamitatibus obruebantur: adeóq; in his verbis, τί μισήσαιν οἱ βαπτιζόμενοι ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν; ejusmodi putat deductionem esse ad absurdum: Si mortui non resurgunt, frustra tot tantósque labores subeunt perferúntque pro mortuis, i. e. pro fidelibus, quoniam nulla foret harum perpessionum retributio. Electos verò vocari mortuos existimat per Ironiam, quia, juxta erroneam adversariorum opinionem, pro mortuis & nunquam resurrecturis revera erant habendi.
units.tr: X. Anna Maria à Schurman, the outstanding light [ὑπερέχον φέγγος], the most noble glory of the Belgians and of deeper learning, thinks otherwise. In her letter to Jacob Lydius, she refers our passage to the ministers of Christ, who, while they kept watch unceasingly over the spreading of the Churches, were overwhelmed in that age by the greatest persecutions and calamities. Thus, in these words, she thinks what will those who are baptized for the dead do [τί ποιήσουσιν οἱ βαπτιζόμενοι ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν;] is a deduction to absurdity: If the dead do not rise, they undergo and endure so many and great labours in vain for the dead, that is, for the faithful, since there would be no return for these sufferings. She thinks the elect are called dead by irony, because, according to the mistaken opinion of the adversaries, they were in truth to be held as dead and never to rise.

units.la: XI. Pia quidem est & egregia isthæc ab admiranda elegantissimi ingenii sagacitate profecta animadversio, non tamen nullis obnoxia incommodis. Nam 1. insolens merito videtur viro haud ignorati nominis in tam exiguo orationis themate confluxus gemini tropi, & quidem ejusmodi, qui rarissime usurpatur, cum planissime loqui amet Apostolus, quando de iis, quas ad aedificationem Ecclesiae sustinebant, perpessionibus loquitur, ut intelligerent Corinthij aliique, mortem in Apostolis agere, vitam vero in illis, 2. Cor. IV. 12. 2. Ironia sicubi sedem aliquam incolit, suo statim se prodit indicio, nec difficulter ex orationis circumstantiis ejus ratio colligi potest: at hic nullum ejus apparet vestigium, quin potius ratio postulare videtur, ut ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν explicetur de mortuis proprie dictis, praesertim si nomen νεκροὶ in medio versu sine articulo positum cum eodem in principio & fine versus cum articulo posito comparemus hunc in modum: Quid facient qui baptizantur pro his vel illis mortuis, si nulli plane mortui, & consequenter nec illi, in quorum gratiam vivi baptizantur, sunt revicturi? 3. Factum eorum, qui pro mortuis baptizabantur, distinguit Apostolus a tropico calamitatum baptismo, quo inundabantur antistites coelestis veritatis, de quo versu 30. agere incipit, ubi, ut commentatores plerique omnes consentiunt conscicuntque, novam pro resurrectione & a priori distinctam urget rationem, vel, si anaphoram in particula ti spectes, novam rationis partem annectendam praecedenti parti & rationi, ut ex utraque integra haec oratio confletur: Corpora mortalium ad vitae munera revocatum iri clarissima elucet significatio ex praelustribus fidelium exemplis, quorum alii propter hanc resurrectionis spem baptizantur pro mortuis: rursum alii, ac nos in primis Ecclesiarum propagatores, eandem ob spem omnia pericula & labores audacter adimus, imo invadimus. Conf. th. 9. rat. 2.
units.tr: XI. This indeed is a pious and excellent observation, springing from the admirable sagacity of a most elegant mind, yet it is not free from some disadvantages. For first, it seems rightly strange to a man of no small name that two tropes should come together in so short a theme of speech, and that of a kind which is very rarely used, since the Apostle loves to speak quite plainly when he speaks of the sufferings he bore for the building up of the Church, so that the Corinthians and others understood that death works in the apostles, but life in you (2 Cor. IV. 12). 2. Irony, wherever it dwells, straightway betrays itself by its own sign, and its reason can not be hard to gather from the circumstances of the speech. But here no trace of it appears; rather, the reason seems to demand that for the dead [ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν] be explained of the dead properly so called, especially if we compare the word νεκροὶ placed without the article in the middle of the verse with the same word placed with the article at the beginning and end of the verse, in this way: What will those do who are baptized for these or those dead, if the dead are in no way at all going to rise, and consequently neither are those in whose favour the living are baptized going to rise again? 3. The Apostle distinguishes the deed of those who were baptized for the dead from the figurative baptism of calamities, with which the leaders of heavenly truth were overwhelmed, and of which he begins to speak at v. 30. There, as nearly all the commentators agree, he urges a new reason for the resurrection, distinct from the former. Or, if you look to the anaphora in the particle ti, it is a new part of the reasoning to be added to the preceding part, so that from both together this whole discourse is made up: that mortal bodies will be recalled to the functions of life is shown most clearly by the illustrious examples of the faithful, some of whom are baptized for the dead on account of this hope of resurrection; and again others, and we above all the propagators of the Churches, boldly undertake and even rush upon all dangers and labours for the same hope. Conf. th. 9. rat. 2.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Hactenus interpretationes eorum, quibus Metaphorica arridet verbi βαπτίζεσθαι acceptio, ponderasse suffecerit: ordo est deinceps, an forte Synecdochica ejusdem verbi notio, qua pro Sacramento baptismi Theologice usurpatur, quamque verborum domina consuetudo usitatissimam voluit esse & paene propriam, huc quadret, dispicere. Eunt autem illius quoque assertores mirabile admodum inter se diversi. Alii enim de vicario baptismo, alii de baptismi pro refrigerio charorum susceptione, alii de baptismo Clinicorum, alii de baptismo sepulchrali, alii de baptismo ad officium certum quibusdam martyribus debitum suscepto, alii de nominum in collatione baptismi impositione, alii denique de baptismo in genere sermonem esse contendunt.
units.tr: It will be enough to have weighed the interpretations of those who favour the metaphorical sense of the verb βαπτίζεσθαι. The next question is whether the synecdochical sense of the same verb, in which it is used theologically for the sacrament of baptism, and which custom, the mistress of words, has made very common and almost proper, fits here. Its advocates differ from one another remarkably. Some contend that the passage speaks of vicarious baptism, others of baptism undertaken for the refreshment of loved ones, others of baptism of the sick-bed, others of sepulchral baptism, others of baptism undertaken for a certain office owed to certain martyrs, others of the imposition of names at the administration of baptism, and others finally of baptism in general.

units.la: XIII. Vica-
units.tr: XIII. Vica-

units.la: XIII. Vicarij baptismatû patroni verba Apostoli ita exponunt: Quid facient qui baptizantur ἀντὶ τῶν νεκρῶν, loco & vice mortuorum? Hæc nempe eos tenet opinio, Apostolum respicere perversam eorum consuetudinem, qui, ubi quempiam subita mors baptismo privâsset, vivum aliquem mortui feretro suppositum pro eo baptizare soliti sunt. Vecordiam hanc Epiphanius hær.28. Cerinthianis sive Merinthianis; Chrysostomus homil.40. in 1.Cor. (ut & Lamb. Danæus comm.in c.22. l.August.de hæref.ad Quodvultd.p.67.) Marcionistis seu Marcionitis tribuit, cujus verba ex Sim. Grynæi translatione adpingere luber: Ita a. ille: Cùm quis apud ipsos Marcionitas initiatus obit, unum aliquem sub mortui lectum recondunt, mortuum circumstant, alloquuntur, rogant, velitne baptizari. Deinde cùm nil respondeat, is qui subtus latet pro illo respondet, baptizari velle: eum deinceps pro mortuo baptizant, sic quemadmodum in scena fieri solet ludentes. Eadem habet Theophylactus ad h.l. Hanc corruptelam, quam etiam apud Corinthios invaluisse aliqui volunt, Apostolum designare, & vice argumenti πρὸς ἀνθρώπων proferre autumant Tertull. l. 5. adv. Marc. c. 10. & de resurr. carn. c.48. Ambros. aut quisquis est, qui sub ejus nomine ad h.l. legitur, Isid. Clarius, Zegerus, Grotius: annot. ad h. l. Camero myroth. Evang. p. 229. Iac. Laurentius in Paulo ἀλυσονήτῳ loc.29.p.440.441. nec abnuunt Zuinglius annot.ad h.l. & Bulling. comm.in 1.Cor.XV.
units.tr: XIII. The patrons of vicarious baptism explain the Apostle's words thus: What will they do who are baptized ἀντὶ τῶν νεκρῶν, in the place and stead of the dead? Their opinion is that the Apostle has in view the perverse custom of those who, when sudden death had prevented someone from being baptized, used to baptize a living man in his place, placing him under the coffin of the dead person. Epiphanius, Haer. 28, attributes this folly to the Cerinthians or Merinthians; Chrysostom, Homily 40 on 1 Corinthians (as also Lambert Danaeus, Commentary on chapter 22, and Augustine, On Heresies, to Quodvultdeus, p. 67) attributes it to the Marcionites or Marcionists. I wish to set down his words in Simon Grynaeus's translation. He writes: When someone among them, the Marcionites, dies after being initiated, they hide some man under the dead man's couch. They stand round the corpse, address it, and ask whether it wishes to be baptized. Then, when it answers nothing, the man who lies hidden beneath answers for it that it wishes to be baptized; then they baptize him on behalf of the dead man, just as is usually done when people play in a stage show. Theophylact has the same account on this passage. Some hold that the Apostle means this abuse, which they say had also taken hold among the Corinthians, and they claim that he brings it forward as an argument ad hominem [πρὸς ἀνθρώπων]: Tertullian, On the Five Books against Marcion, 5.10, and On the Resurrection of the Flesh, c. 48; Ambrose, or whoever it is that is read under his name on this passage; Isidore of Pelusium; Clarius; Zegerus; Grotius, Annotations on this passage; Cameron, Myrothecium Evangelicum, p. 229; Jacob Laurentius, On Paul, ἀλυσονήτῳ, loc. 29, pp. 440–441. Nor do Zwingli, Annotations on this passage, and Bullinger, Commentary on 1 Corinthians 15, deny it.

units.la: XIV. Verùm in alia omnia transeundum sibi duxerunt viri, qui ad illustrem hominum memoriam inclaruerunt, alii, nec forte inconsultò. Nam 1. neque Marcionitæ, neque Cerinthiani exemplum Apostolo exhibere potuerunt. Non Marcionitæ, tum quia eorum antesignanus Marcion altero demum à N.C. seculo suas in Ecclesiæ agrum sevit corruptelas, tum quia iidem cum Cerdonianis resurrectionem carnis negârunt liquidò. Non Cerinthiani, tum quia, licèt superante adhuc Paulo funestum proferre caput & facere vestigia cœperit coryphæus eorum Cerinthus, in ambiguo tamen relinquitur, an Apostolicam ante obitum Pauli manifestè deseruerit Ecclesiam, cùm eum mortuo Nerone, cujus gladium cruentavit Paulus, Domitiano rerum gubernacula tractante, per Asiam minorem & Syriam (vid. Danæus comm. in c.8.l. Aug.de hær.p.28.) venenum suum sparsisse, & adversum ejus, ut & Ebionis, dementiam Johannem, qui solus ex Apostolis supererat, Episcoporum Asiæ rogatu, divinam Christi nativitatem ab aliis paulò tectius relatam diserte & luculenter in Evangelio suo postremum edito exposuisse, rerum explicatores tradant: tum quia multis suspectum est, an Cerinthianis, qui velut observantissimi legalium ceremoniarum cultores circumcisionem retinuerunt, vicarium baptisma vere tribuatur: tum quia Apostolus anilem illam superstitionem, si suo jam tempore inolevisset, absque ullo vel levissimo ac perfunctorio dissensu publico minime transmisisset: tum denique quia ex facto clandestino & Apocrypho, quale illud Cerinthianorum nonnulli faciunt, argumentari Apostolum in Epistola Catholica supra fidem est. In causæ igitur suæ patrocinium non Apostolus sive Marcionitarum, sive Cerinthianorum somniationem, sed illi hunc Pauli locum arripuerunt & sinistro sensu perverterunt.
units.tr: XIV. But other men, who have become famous in the memory of illustrious people, thought they should pass on to other views, and perhaps not without good reason. For, first, neither the Marcionites nor the Cerinthians could have provided the Apostle with an example. Not the Marcionites: first, because their standard-bearer Marcion sowed his corruptions in the field of the Church only in the second century after Christ; second, because the same people clearly denied the resurrection of the flesh together with the Cerdonians. Not the Cerinthians: first, because although Cerinthus, their chief, began to raise his deadly head and set his footsteps while Paul was still alive, it remains uncertain whether he had openly deserted the Apostolic Church before Paul's death. The historians of these events relate that after the death of Nero, whose sword Paul had reddened with blood, while Domitian held the reins of government, Cerinthus scattered his poison through Asia Minor and Syria (see Danaeus, Commentary on chapter 8; Augustine, On Heresies, p. 28), and that against his madness, and that of Ebion, John, who alone of the Apostles still survived, at the request of the bishops of Asia, set out in plain and clear terms in his Gospel, published last, the divine nativity of Christ, which others had related somewhat more obscurely. Second, because it is doubted by many whether the Cerinthians, who as the most devoted observers of the legal ceremonies retained circumcision, really ascribed a vicarious baptism to themselves. Third, because the Apostle, if that old-womanish superstition had already taken root in his own time, would by no means have let it pass without some public dissent, however slight and cursory. Finally, because it is beyond belief that the Apostle should argue in a Catholic Epistle from a clandestine and apocryphal fact, such as some of the Cerinthians make this one. So the Apostle, in defence of his cause, did not take up the Marcionite or Cerinthian dream; rather those men seized upon this passage of Paul and twisted it to a wrong sense.

units.la: 2. Argumenta ad hominem
units.tr: 2. Arguments ad hominem

units.la: tum demum stringunt, quum ab ejus, qui cum res est, sunt persuasione. At vero apud Corinthios vanum istum & insanum baptizandi alios pro defunctis ritum increbuisse, verisimilitudine caret. An putamus, verba sunt Calvini comm. in Ep. Paul. p. 367. notatu dignissima, si talis corruptela invaluisset apud Corinthios, Apostolum, quum singula prope eorum vitia taxaverit, de hoc fuisse taciturum? Superius ritus quosdam reprehendit non adeo magni momenti: de velandis mulierum capitibus & aliis ejus generis præcipere non gravatus est: vitiosam Cænæ administrationem non reprehendit tantum, sed acerrime exagitavit: unde tam fœda Baptismi profanatione nullum interea verbum dixisset, quæ tamen gravitate præponderabat? Et paucis interjectis: Sed demum potuisse subticere: quid dum eam nominat? Obsecro, an verisimile est, sacrilegium, quo Baptismus inquinaretur ac traheretur in abusum prorsus magicum, Apostolum protulisse vice argumenti, & non uno saltem verbulo notâsse vitium? Quum de rebus non maximis agitur, parenthesin tamen inserit, se loqui secundum hominem: an hic parenthesi non erat aptior locus & opportunior? nunc quod sine ulla reprehensione commemorat, quis non accipiat tanquam licitum? Hæc Calvinus.
units.tr: Such arguments are then compelling only when they come from the conviction of the very person with whom the matter is concerned. But that this empty and insane rite of baptizing others on behalf of the dead had grown up among the Corinthians lacks probability. Do we think, these are the words of Calvin in his Commentary on the Pauline Epistles, p. 367, most worthy of notice, that if such a corruption had taken hold among the Corinthians, the Apostle, who has censured almost each of their faults, would have kept silent about this? Earlier he rebukes certain rites that are not of great importance; he did not hesitate to give instructions about covering women's heads and other matters of that kind. He not only rebukes the faulty administration of the Supper but attacks it most sharply. Would he then have said no word meanwhile about so foul a profanation of Baptism, which nevertheless outweighs them all in seriousness? And a little further on, after some interjections: But suppose he could have been silent: what of the moment when he names it? I beg you, is it likely that the Apostle would have brought forward, as an argument, a sacrilege by which Baptism was defiled and dragged into a wholly magical abuse, and would not have marked the fault by at least one little word? When he deals with matters that are not of the highest importance, he nevertheless inserts a parenthesis, saying that he speaks according to men; was not a parenthesis more apt and more fitting in this place? Now what he mentions without any rebuke, who would not take as lawful? So far Calvin.

units.la: 3. Apostolum ad astruendam veritatem plumbeo hoc mucrone certâsse vero non est consentaneum: tum quia Prophetæ & Apostoli non solent falsa assumere ad corroborandum verum, sicuti nec facere mala suadent, ut eveniant bona: tum quia error pro obtinenda veritate ἐπικρίσια συνώνη est, præsertim ubi illa suis se munire copiis abundè potest.
units.tr: 3. It is not consistent for the Apostle to have fought for the establishing of truth with this leaden sword: first, because Prophets and Apostles are not accustomed to take up falsehoods to strengthen the truth, any more than they advise doing evil so that good may come of it; second, because an error used to win the truth is a kind of accomplice [ἐπικρίσια συνώνη], especially where the truth can amply defend itself with its own forces.

units.la: XV. Alium adolescentis Christianorum Ecclesiæ errorem in textûs nostri explanatione sub aspectum protrahit Illustriss. Jos. Scaliger Critic. S.T.VII.p.3098.3099: qui de baptizatis pro refrigerio charorum ab Apostolo agi arbitratur. Opinio illius συλλήβδην hæc est: Christiani veteres animas piorum, impiorum (martyribus, quos uno saltu rectà in paradisum deferri æstimabant, exceptis) in centro terræ, tanq. in quodam conceptaculo, expectare diem judicii putabant, quod Tertull. eleganter dixit in candida expectare diem judicii. Hinc magna incessebat eos solicitudo charorum suorum, qui jam defuncti eo in carcere anxio extremæ diei desiderio conflictabantur. Quare pro iis annuâ die offerebant (quæ oblatio εὐχαριστία erat, non ἱλαστικὴ, &, ut ait August. humanitatis officium, non salutis præsidium) &, dicente Tertull. adpostulabant aliquod refrigerium in die resurrectionis, quod qualè sit, ipsi fortassis nesciebant. Antiquius verò, putà propius Apostolorum tempora, pro eodem eorundem refrigerio baptizabantur annuatim, Calendis sc. Februariis, quo die Dominum ipsum à Johanne baptizatum vetustiores conjecturabant, quémque, ut vim verbi φωτίζεσθαι, quod erat βαπτίζεσθαι, testarentur, non solùm φωσφόρον ἡμέραν vocabant, sed & cereos aut lucernas eodem accendebant, quæ φωτοχηΐα, licèt recentiores ἐπιφάνια seu βάπτισμα κυριακὸν in VI. Januarii rejecerint, Kal. tamen Feb. remansit, & propter solenne Purificationis in perendinum translata hodièque durat in Ecclesiis, quæ errores Patrum doctrinæ Christi præferre solent. Ab hac jam baptismi pro refrigerio charorum susceptione argumentari Apostolum, & quamvis vesaniam non laudet, eos tamen, qui baptizabantur pro mortuis, ut refrigerium habeant in die resurrectionis, sui tamen obliti resurrectionem negabant, suo sibi jugulare gladio, ille eruditionis aliger pronuntiat.
units.tr: XV. Another error of the young Christian Church is brought into view in the explanation of our text by the most illustrious Joseph Scaliger, Critical Writings, Sacred Texts, VII, pp. 3098–3099, who thinks that the Apostle is speaking of men baptized for the refreshment of their loved ones. His opinion in brief is this: the early Christians thought that the souls of the pious and the impious (except the martyrs, whom they believed were carried straight away into paradise in one leap) waited in the centre of the earth, as though in some receptacle, for the day of judgement; Tertullian aptly called this to await the day of judgement in a bright place. Hence a great anxiety troubled them about their loved ones, who, now dead, were struggling in that prison with anxious longing for the last day. So they offered sacrifices for them once a year (this offering was a thanksgiving [εὐχαριστία], not a propitiation [ἱλαστικὴ], and, as Augustine says, a duty of humanity, not a protection of salvation), and, as Tertullian says, they asked for some refreshment on the day of the resurrection, though what sort it would be they perhaps did not know themselves. Earlier still, that is nearer to the times of the Apostles, they were baptized every year for the same refreshment of the same dead, on the Calends of February, the day on which the older writers supposed the Lord himself was baptized by John. To attest the force of the word to be enlightened [φωτίζεσθαι], which is the same as to be baptized [βαπτίζεσθαι], they called this day not only the light-bearing day [φωσφόρον ἡμέραν] but also lit candles or lamps on it. These rites of light-bringing [φωτοχηΐα], although later writers moved the Epiphany or the Lord's baptism [ἐπιφάνια seu βάπτισμα κυριακὸν] to 6 January, remained on the Calends of February, and because of the solemn Purification, transferred to the day after tomorrow, it still lasts today in churches, which are accustomed to prefer the errors of the Fathers to the doctrine of Christ. Scaliger, that man armed with learning, declares that from this baptism undertaken for the refreshment of loved ones the Apostle argues; and although he does not praise the madness, nevertheless those who were baptized for the dead, so that they might have refreshment on the day of the resurrection, while forgetful of themselves, denied the resurrection, thereby cutting their own throat with their own sword.

units.la: XVI. Erudita quidem illa, judice Heinsio Exerc. S. ad N. T. p. 407. nec tamen in eruditorum theatro, quantum perspicere datur, palmarem impetraverè applausum. Nam 1. an turpis iste de baptismo nævus in venusta Ecclesiæ virginis facie apparuerit, μέγα λίαν ζήτημα. Non existimamus, ait Cloppenb. disp. Theol. de sent. h.l. Patrum illud anile deliramentum, quod cumulárunt Pontificii suis hæresibus de satisfactione pro mortuorum animabus liberandis ex carcere Utopico Purgatorii per baptismum Metaphoricum lacrymarum & poenitentia, qui suscipiatur orando, jejunando, beneficentiam exercendo, proque mortuis sese afflictando, Apostolo in mentem venisse. Quod deliramentum siejus sit antiquitatis, ut jam pullulárit Apostolus viventibus, non eo arreptum esse Apostoli argumentum censemus, sed contra arripuisse & detorsisse homines imperitos & instabiles hunc Pauli & Pet. 1. Pet. III. 19. locum ἀσνόητον. 2. An eo errore laboraverint in specie Corinthii, & in Corinthiis ii, qui ad Philosophorum placita adulterárunt resurrectionis dogma, etiam atque etiam dubitabile. 3. Cur Apostolus errorem tam perniciosum sub baptismi nomine grassari permiserit & eundem politica sepelierit ἀμνησίᾳ: etiam ab eo argumentum, apud Ecclesiam praesertim & fideles, ad quos scripsit, desumserit, mirationem cuiam non abs re faciat. Redi sis ad th. 14.
units.tr: XVI. That learned theory, to the judgement of Heinsius, Sacred Exercises on the New Testament, p. 407, has not, so far as one can see, won the palm of applause in the theatre of scholars. For, first, whether that shameful blemish on baptism appeared on the lovely face of the virgin Church is a very great question. We do not think, says Cloppenburg, Theological Disputation on the opinion on this passage, that the Apostle had in mind that old-womanish nonsense of the Fathers, which the Papists heaped up with their heresies about satisfaction for freeing the souls of the dead from the Utopian prison of Purgatory, through a metaphorical baptism of tears and repentance, which is undertaken by praying, fasting, practising beneficence, and afflicting oneself on behalf of the dead. If that nonsense is so old that it had already sprouted in the lifetime of the Apostle, we do not judge that the Apostle took up his argument from it; rather, unlearned and unstable men seized upon this passage of Paul and of 1 Peter 3:19 and twisted it into an unintelligible [ἀσνόητον] sense. Second, whether the Corinthians in particular, and among the Corinthians those who corrupted the doctrine of the resurrection with the tenets of the philosophers, were infected with that error, is doubtful again and again. Third, why the Apostle would have allowed so pernicious an error to spread under the name of baptism, and would have buried it with political forgetfulness [ἀμνησίᾳ], and yet would have drawn his argument from it, especially before the Church and the faithful to whom he wrote, may well provoke some wonder. Return to thesis 14.

units.la: XVII. Cùm itaque Scaligeri quoque expositio familiá summo- veatur, Ἐντάφιον Clinicorum βάπτισμα, ut instituimus, ad considera- tionem vocemus.
units.tr: XVII. Since Scaliger's explanation is also set aside, let us now bring to consideration the entaphion [Ἐντάφιον] of the Clinics, their baptism [βάπτισμα], as we proposed.

units.la: Solebant antiquitus Catechumeni morbo graviore constricti, imminente lethali periculo, πρὸ τῆς πλευτῆς baptismum petere, tanquam itineris extremi viaticum, ne absque publico salutis testimonio ex hac vita emigrarent, qui, quia ἐν τῇ κλίνῃ lectulis affixi aquâ affundebantur, Clinici inde seu Lectulari, Peripatetici à Cypriano l. 4. Ep. 7. ad Magnum oppositi, audiebant. Horum de baptismo qui accipiunt Apostolum, verba ejus ita vertunt: Quid facient qui baptizantur vel ὡσεὶ νεκροὶ jam quasi mortui, seu moribundi: vel sub mortis tempus: vel pro statu mortuorum, ut illic bene habeant & resurrectionem gloriosam consequantur. Præitque hanc ἑρμηνείαν Epiphan. hær. 28. de Cerinth. ut videre est Observ. S. Clariss. Dn. Suic. c. 3. p. 69. Ei astipulatores se præbent plurimi magnæ famæ & eruditionis viri, Calvin. comm. in Ep. Paul. p. 367. Gualth. Archet. homil. in Ep. Apost. p. 147. Hemming. comm. in Epist. Apost. p. 238. Iac. Cappellus annot. ad h. l. Estius comm. in h. l. Marlorat. Expos. Eccl. in h. l. Corn. à Lapide comm. in Epist. Paul. p. 327. b. alii, quos nominare haud attinet.
units.tr: In ancient times catechumens who were held fast by a more serious illness, with deadly danger impending, used to ask for baptism before the end [πρὸ τῆς τελευτῆς], as a viaticum for the last stage of the journey, so that they would not depart from this life without a public witness of salvation. Because they were water-poured while lying on their beds [ἐν τῇ κλίνῃ], they were called Clinics, or Bedridden, and were opposed by Cyprian (Ep. 4, 7, to Magnus) as Peripatetics. Those who take the Apostle's words about baptism translate them thus: What will they do who are baptized, if the dead [ὡσεὶ νεκροί] rise, that is, as if already dead or dying; or at the time of death; or for the state of the dead, so that they may fare well there and obtain a glorious resurrection? Epiphanius (haer. 28, on the Cerinthians) led the way in this interpretation, as may be seen in the Observationes sacrae of the most distinguished Mr. Suicer, c. 3, p. 69. Many men of great reputation and learning side with it: Calvin (comm. in Ep. Paul., p. 367), Gualther (Archetypus homiliarum in Ep. Apost., p. 147), Hemmingius (comm. in Epist. Apost., p. 238), Jacob Cappellus (annot. ad h. l.), Estius (comm. in h. l.), Marlorat (Expos. Eccl. in h. l.), Cornelius à Lapide (comm. in Epist. Paul., p. 327 b), and others whom it is not worth naming.

units.la: XVIII. Verùm neque hæc explicatio ponitur extra tela, quod di- citur, & pulverem.
units.tr: XVIII. But this explanation is not beyond the reach of weapons, as they say, and dust.

units.la: Nam 1. obstat ei conciliatio phraseos, tum quia ὡσεὶ νεκροὶ & ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν Synonyma esse vix possunt: tum quia Latinæ præpositioni Pro in hoc usu, quo dicimus habere pro derelicto, Græcam ὑπερ̀ non respondere οἱ τῶν γραμματικῶν παιδίςς nõrūnt:tum quia ὑπερ̀ τῶν νεκρῶν reddere cum Cappello sub mortis tempu. nimis violentum: tum quia vox νεκροὶ nullibi abstractè solum statum mortuorum, sine connotatione eorum qui in isto statu sunt, designat, quum phrasis resurgere ex mortuis non de resurrectione universali, quæ resurrectio mortuorum nominatur, sed semper tum usurpetur, quando quis alios mortuos in morte relinquit: tum denique quia Apostolus loqui de iis qui baptizabantur pro aliis, non pro se ipsis, series contextus innuit.
units.tr: For, first, its reading of the phrase is an obstacle. The expressions as if dead [ὡσεὶ νεκροὶ] and for the dead [ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν] can hardly be synonyms. The Latin preposition pro, in the sense in which we say to hold for abandoned, does not correspond to the Greek ὑπέρ, as schoolboys of grammar know. To render ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν with Cappellus as at the time of death is too forced. The word νεκροί nowhere denotes the mere abstract state of the dead without reference to those who are in that state. The phrase to rise from the dead is never used of the general resurrection, which is called the resurrection of the dead, but always when someone leaves others dead behind him. Finally, the sense of the context shows that the Apostle is speaking of those who were baptized on behalf of others, not on their own behalf.

units.la: 2. Morem illum requirendi baptismum in agone, qui trahebat perniciem veniens in ævum, superstite Paulo receptum fuisse nusquam neque pictum, neque scriptum, cùm è diverso Apostolos baptismatis ritu conversos suos confestim initiâsse, nec longas nexuisse moras, ex Actis eorum constet. Probabilius ergo statuitur, morem illum post Apostolorum tum excessum, tum defectum, seculo vel secundo, quo Victor Episcopus Rom. Catholicum baptisma nonnisi die Paschatis extra casum necessitatis celebrari decrevit, uti nos informant Magdeburg.cent.2.c.6 p.m.111. & Stratem.theat.hist.p.396. vel tertio; quo Cyprianus Carthaginensis Episcopus, cùm existeret quæstio, utrum baptismus Clinicorum aspersione duntaxat legitimè perageretur, patrocinium eorum suscepit, l.4.Epist.7.ad Magnum; irrepsisse, & eam in superstitionem abiisse, ut baptismi usum plurimi vel ex metu, ne gratiam in baptismo perceptam, surrepentibus novis delictis, denuo perderent, vel aliis de causis, cujusmodi in Constantino M. fuit desiderium baptismi in Jordane fluvio suscipiendi, usque ad extremum vitæ spatium consultò distulerint: quibus tamen, si forte convaluerunt, omnis Ecclesiasticæ promotionis spes præcisa fuit, ut alii exemplum sumerent cautius mercandi & maturius baptismum solicitandi.
units.tr: Second, that custom of seeking baptism in the struggle, which brought ruin into the age to come, is nowhere attested, either in pictures or in writing, while Paul was still living. On the contrary, it is plain from the Acts that the Apostles straightway initiated those converted to them by the rite of baptism and did not allow long delays. It is therefore more probable that the custom crept in after the Apostles' death and failure, either in the second century, when Victor, bishop of Rome, decreed that Catholic baptism should be celebrated only on Easter day and apart from cases of necessity (as Magdeburg Centuries, cent. 2, c. 6, p. 111, and Stratemann, theatrum historicum, p. 396, inform us), or in the third century, when Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, took up the cause of the Clinics, when the question arose whether the baptism of the bedridden was lawfully performed by sprinkling alone (Ep. 4, 7, to Magnus). By then it had degenerated into superstition, so that many deferred deliberately, until the last span of life, the use of baptism: some out of fear that, if new sins crept in, they would lose again the grace received in baptism; others for other reasons, such as the desire of Constantine the Great to be baptized in the river Jordan. Yet if such men happened to recover, all hope of ecclesiastical advancement was cut off, so that others might take the example of being more cautious in putting off baptism and more timely in seeking it.

units.la: 3. Argumentum à baptismo Clinicorum adscitum pondere destituitur & momento, cùm οἱ ἐξ ἐναντίας baptismum morituris per solam peccatorum remissionem, & quod ad animum non mediocri emolumento esse, etiam si corpora non resurgant, excipere potuerint. Neque enim in hypothesin, quòd baptismi fructus ad corpora etiam redundet, adversariorum animi fuissent propensi, & si illâ nixus fuisset Apostolus, controversum probâsset per æquè controversum.
units.tr: Third, the argument drawn from the baptism of the Clinics loses its weight and force, since our opponents could have taken baptism for the dying as bringing only the remission of sins, and as being of no small advantage to the soul even if the bodies do not rise. Nor would the opponents have been inclined to the hypothesis that the fruit of baptism also overflows to the bodies; and if the Apostle had relied on that, he would have proved a disputed point by an equally disputed one.

units.la: XIX. 'A lectulis moribundorum provolvamur ad sepulchra mor- tuorum, ubi se nobis objicit alia quædam baptizandi Christianos cere- monia,
units.tr: XIX. Let us turn from the beds of the dying to the tombs of the dead, where another ceremony of baptizing Christians presents itself to us,

units.la: monia, quâ nempe in sepulcretis mortuorum, inprimis martyrum, & ad eorum ossa vel tumbas, sive ibi fons aliquis fuerit, sive baptisterium fabrefactum, baptizabantur, ut se mortuorum causæ hyperaspistas esse & cum Christo mori peccato publicè profiterentur, fidem quoque suam partim de resurrectione mortuorum, partim de spirituali baptizatorum vivorum cum membris unius ejusdemque corporis mystici consociatione redderent contestatam. Ad particularem hunc in delectu loci ritum qui volunt alludere Apostolum, verba ejus ita transferunt: Quid facient qui baptizantur ὑπερ̀ τῶν νεκρῶν supra mortuos, h.e. supra cadavera sepulchris commissa seu super monumenta defunctorum. Hæc διάνοια placet Luthero in verf. Germ. & expos. h.l. à quo denso agmine stant, qui ab eo ἐπωνυμίαν habent plerique, Centuriatores Magdeburgici cent. 1. l. 2. c. 4. p. 247. 464. & c. 6. p. 490. Osiander ad h.l. Sim. Pauli method. LL. doctr. Christ. part. 4. meth. 35. p. 9. Hunnius comm. ad h. l. Pfeilius clav. Theol. art. 17. p. 613. Glassius Philol. S. l. 3. tr. 6. p. 559. nec non ex ἰουστίνου πίστεως consecraneis Piscator annot. ad h.l. Bucanus Instit. Theol. loc. 47. p. 681. 682. Pastor Lex: N. T. in voc. νέκυς & ὑπὲρ p. 478. & 672. Celeb. Marefcoll. Theol. loc. 14. p. 559. deniq; etiam Anabaptista hist. de bapt. Germ. p. 100.
units.tr: namely, that Christians were baptized in the burial grounds of the dead, above all of the martyrs, and at their bones or tombs, whether there was a spring there or a baptistery built for the purpose. In doing so they publicly professed that they were defenders of the cause of the dead, and that they died with Christ to sin; and they also gave witness of their faith, partly concerning the resurrection of the dead, partly concerning the spiritual union of the living baptized with the members of one and the same mystical body. Those who want the Apostle to allude to this rite of choosing a particular place translate his words thus: What will they do who are baptized over [ὑπὲρ] the dead, that is, over corpses committed to tombs, or over the monuments of the departed. This interpretation pleases Luther, in his German version and in his exposition of this passage, and behind him stand in close ranks those who take their name mostly from him: the Magdeburg Centuriators (cent. 1, l. 2, c. 4, pp. 247, 464, and c. 6, p. 490), Osiander (ad h. l.), Simon Paulus (method. LL. doctr. Christ., part 4, meth. 35, p. 9), Hunnius (comm. ad h. l.), Pfeilius (clavis theol., art. 17, p. 613), Glassius (Philologia sacra, l. 3, tr. 6, p. 559). Likewise from the associates of Justin's faith, Piscator (annot. ad h. l.), Bucanus (Instit. Theol., loc. 47, pp. 681, 682), Pastor (Lex. N. T., under νέκυς and ὑπέρ, p. 478 and p. 672), the celebrated Maresius (Theol., loc. 14, p. 559); and finally, even the Anabaptist (hist. de bapt., Germ., p. 100).

units.la: XX. Tametsi autem plausibilis ista videatur interpretatio, nondum tamen ad extremam manum suâ perfectione est perducta. Etenim 1. solido historicæ veritatis tibicine non est fulta. Incertum certè, an simplices martyrum memoriæ; quæ fuerunt partim Encomiastica seu panegyricæ eorum laudationes bonâ intentione ad alios è veterno vitiorum excitandos & ad similem virtutis excellentiam inflammandos institutæ, partim Eucharistica Dei pro eorum constantia donisque celebrationes, partim preces ad Deum pro simili gratia & consummata ipsorum gloria ardenter fusæ, partim denique ut mutuæ charitatis, ita communis fidei & spei omnium Christianorum testificationes; ætate Apostolorum cœperint: Smyrnensis enim Ecclesiæ fratres primos doctoris sui Polycarpi, viri Apostolici, qui circiter A.D. 170. sub M. Antonino Vero (errare nanq; Socratem asserentem Polycarpum sub Gordiano passum esse l. 5. c. 22. satis crassè, monent Magdeb. cent. 2. c. 10. p. 176.) ætate ad senectutem præcipitatâ Smyrnæ crematus est, natalem cum exultatione & gaudio ad memoriam eorum qui antea certârunt & suturorum exercitationem ac praeparationem celebrâsse, ex literis eorum ad Ponti Ecclesias datis, quæ extant apud Eusebh.hist.Eccl.l.4.c.15. palàm evadit. Incertum, an martyrum memoriæ, Apostolis adhuc spiritum è cœlo ducentibus, viguerint etiam in baptismi susceptione. Incertissimum, an viguerint cum ritu superaddito, quem postulat expositio particulæ ὑπὲρ per ὑπεράνω, qui non Apostolicam simplicitatem, sed περισσωπολη ψίαν seu nimiam mortuorum admirationem & superstitionem olet, quam Apostolus haud dissimulaturus fuisset. 2. Quoniam igitur Catechumeni cæmeteria seligere & in iis se baptizandos sistere potuerunt in honorem maximè & memoriam morte affectorum, argumenti vis pro resurrectione non constat. 3. Quum inter prima Christianæ rei initia flagrârit persecutionum ignis, omnémque tyranni in Christianos rabiem exegerint, ritum illum baptizandi in polyandriis ullibi potuisse exerceri non est verisimile.
units.tr: XX. Although this interpretation may seem plausible, it has not yet been brought to its final polish, since it is not supported by a firm prop of historical truth. First, it is uncertain whether the simple memorials of the martyrs began in the time of the Apostles. Some of these were encomiastic or panegyrical praises of them, set up with good intention to rouse others from their torpor and to kindle a similar excellence of virtue; some were Eucharistic celebrations of God for their constancy and the gifts bestowed on them; some were prayers poured out ardently to God for similar grace and for the completed glory of the martyrs; and some, finally, were testimonies of mutual charity and of the common faith and hope of all Christians. That these began with the Apostles is clear from the letters of the brethren of the Smyrnean Church, sent to the churches of Pontus and preserved in Eusebius (Hist. Eccl., l. 4, c. 15). They there celebrated the birthday of their teacher Polycarp, an apostolic man, who was burned at Smyrna about the year 170 under Marcus Antoninus Verus (the Magdeburg Centuries, cent. 2, c. 10, p. 176, remark that Socrates is quite crudely wrong in saying that Polycarp suffered under Gordian, l. 5, c. 22), when his age was hastening towards old age. They kept it with exultation and joy in memory of those who had fought before, and as a training and preparation for those to come. It is uncertain whether the memories of the martyrs flourished, while the Apostles were still drawing the Spirit from heaven, also at the reception of baptism. It is most uncertain whether they flourished with an added rite, which the explanation of the particle ὑπέρ as ὑπεράνω requires. Such an explanation smells not of apostolic simplicity but of περισσωπολη ψίαν [excessive], that is, of an excessive admiration and superstition for the dead, which the Apostle would hardly have passed over in silence. Second, since catechumens could choose cemeteries and present themselves there to be baptized, especially in honour and memory of those who had died, the force of the argument for the resurrection does not stand. Third, since the fire of persecution blazed among the first beginnings of the Christian cause, and tyrants exercised all their rage against Christians, it is not likely that the rite of baptizing over the common graves could have been practised anywhere.

units.la: XXI. Memorias martyrum in baptismi susceptione recoli solitas restringit vir omni memoria dignissimus Joh. Cloppenburgius syntag.select.Exerc. Theol.p.444.445. non ad locum, sed ad personas & certos quosdam martyres, illos nimirum, qui tum ex Apostolis, tum ex quingentis resurrectionis Christi testibus oculatis martyrio coronati sunt, de quibus sermo inchoatus fuit v.6. continuatus v.11.15.18. & ad quos sermo redit v. 29. sicut ad viventes superstites v.30.31. Illos igitur martyres, siquidem censendi essent ψευδομάρτυρες in causa Dei, non sibi tantum suæ perditionis autores fuisse, sed & iis, qui propter illos baptizabantur, h.e. qui postquàm viventes illos audiissent aut spectâssent morientium in testimonio de Christi resurrectione constantiam, & validissimarum consolationum in morte experientiam, illis magistris gloriabantur, se Christum didicisse, & ad illorum memorias, officio per se pio, baptismum flagitabant, fraudem dedisse, Apostolus, Cloppenburgii sententiâ, inculcat.
units.tr: XXI. The memorials of martyrs customarily recalled at the reception of baptism are restricted by the man most worthy of all memory, Johannes Cloppenburg, Syntag. select. Exerc. Theol. p. 444, 445, not to a place but to certain persons, namely those martyrs who were crowned with martyrdom, both among the Apostles and among the five hundred eyewitnesses of Christ's resurrection. The discussion of them begins at v. 6, continues at vv. 11, 15 and 18, and returns at v. 29, and at vv. 30 and 31 it turns to the survivors who are still alive. Cloppenburg's view is that the Apostle insists that those martyrs, if indeed they were to be counted false witnesses in God's cause, were the authors not only of their own ruin but also of the ruin of those who were baptized on their account. That is, after they had heard or seen living and dying witnesses of Christ's resurrection, and had observed their constancy and their experience of very strong consolation in death, they gloried in those teachers, saying that they had learned Christ from them, and, to honour the memory of those men, begged for baptism, a duty pious in itself. The Apostle, on Cloppenburg's view, charges them with deceit.

units.la: XXII. Ad quam exegesin suffecerit attulisse accuratam Ultrajectinæ Palladis A.M.Schurmanna επικρισιν, quam suppeditat Epist. ejus ad Cloppenb. exarata. Primum non satis solidè, inquit illa, saltem ex hoc cap. probari posse existimem, nonnullos ex illis quingentis fratribus, quos obdormivisse prædicat Apostolus v.6. martyrii coronam consecutos fuisse. Deinde v.11. intelligendum esse de iisdem sive viventibus adhuc, sive jam mortuis, abnuere videtur ipsa series & orationis contextus v.7.8.9.10. & 11. Ubi non agitur de martyribus illis vita modò defunctis, sed de Apostolis tum temporis, cùm S. Paulus haec scriberet, resurrectionem Christi annunciantibus. Idem fere dixerim de v.15. quando ibid. ex falsa haereticorum hypothesi, Apostolos potius, quàm alios quoslibet criminis ψευδομαρτυρίας argui vero consentaneum est. Postremo exempla mihi nunc quidem non occurrunt, quibus certò evinci queat, verba & phrasin Apostolicam ultro admittere hanc interpretationem, τί ποιήσουσιν οἱ βαπτιζόμενοι ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν; nihil aliud denotare, quàm quosdam Christianorum olim & tunc temporis Baptismum recepisse, commotos scil. exemplo istorum Martyrum, qui hanc veritatem proprio sanguine obsignaverant. Huiusque Schurmanna, in cujus judicio haud repugnanter acquiescimus.
units.tr: XXII. For this exegesis it will suffice to bring forward the careful epikrisis of A. M. Schurman of the Utrecht Pallas, which is set out in her letter to Cloppenburg. "First," she says, "I do not think it can be proved solidly enough, at least from this chapter, that some of those five hundred brothers whom the Apostle says fell asleep at v. 6 obtained the crown of martyrdom. Next, v. 11 is to be understood of the same men, whether still living or already dead; the very sequence and context of the discourse at vv. 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11 seems to deny it. For there is discussion not of those martyrs who are merely dead, but of the Apostles of that time, when St Paul was writing this and announcing the resurrection of Christ. I would say much the same of v. 15, since there too, on the false hypothesis of the heretics, it is the Apostles rather than any others who are rightly charged with the crime of false witness." Finally, I do not at present recall examples by which it can be certainly shown that the words and the Apostolic phrasing τί ποιήσουσιν οἱ βαπτιζόμενοι ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν; [what will those do who are baptized for the dead?] readily admit this interpretation, namely that they denote nothing other than that certain Christians, both of old and at that time, received baptism, moved, that is, by the example of those martyrs who had sealed this truth with their own blood. So Schurman, and in her judgement we acquiesce without reluctance.

units.la: XXIII.
