units.tr: XXIII.

units.la: In peculiari semita versatur etiam summus & incomparabilis Heinsius S. Exerc. ad N.T. l.7. c.13 p.407.408. qui argumentari Apostolum existimat a ritu ex circumcisione in Ecclesiam N.T. propagato, quo Christiani plerunque Apostolorum Martyrum, S. Patrum, aut suorum, qui virtute, ac probitate excelluissent, nomen suis imponebant, ut sic vivere, sic superesse viderentur, aut ut, postea resurrecturi, quiescere ac dormire ad tempus crederentur. Quia v. quibus τῶν τεθνεώτων nomina imponebantur, baptizari in defunctorum nomina, quod soli Deo convenit, dici non poterant, ὑπὲρ ἐκείνων, in eorum vel honorem vel memoriam baptizari dicebantur, quod non male nomen defuncti suscitare dicas, alia in reIudaeis usitatum Deut.XXV.v.7. Ruth.IV. v.10. Ex his jam Heinsius hanc extruit paraphrasin: Nam quid illis fiet, aut quid respondebunt, si de resurrectione dubitant, nec eam credunt, qui in mortuorum suos vel baptizant memoriam, vel baptizantur? Resurrectionem enim si non credunt, quare mortuos considerant ut vivos, cùm eorum nomina aut aliis imponant, aut imponi sibi patiantur?
units.tr: Heinsius also walks a peculiar path. He is the most eminent and incomparable man, S. Exerc. ad N.T. l. 7. c. 13 p. 407, 408. He thinks the Apostle argues from the rite, spread into the New Testament Church from circumcision, by which Christians for the most part gave their children the names of Apostolic martyrs, of the Fathers, or of their own people who had excelled in virtue and uprightness, so that such persons might seem to live and to survive, or might be believed to rest and sleep for a time, to rise again later. Because those of the dead [τῶν τεθνεώτων] whose names were given could not be said to be baptized into the names of the dead, which belongs to God alone, they were said to be baptized for them [ὑπὲρ ἐκείνων], in their honour or memory, which you may fairly call raising up the name of the dead, a practice known among the Jews from Deut. XXV. 7 and Ruth IV. 10. From these points Heinsius now builds this paraphrase: For what will happen to those who doubt the resurrection and do not believe it, who either baptize in memory of their dead or allow themselves to be baptized? For if they do not believe in the resurrection, why do they regard the dead as living, since they either give their names to others or suffer their names to be given to themselves?

units.la: XXIV.
units.tr: XXIV.

units.la: Expositio haec, uti censet Laurent. in Paulo p.440. magis erudita ac subtilis est, quàm certa vel etiam multùm probabilis. Nec enim liquet, quâ ratione pro aliquo baptizari idem valeat, quod nomen alicujus accipere in baptismo. De tempore autem, quo Christianis primùm in baptismi impertitione nomina sint imposita, historici certant & adhuc sub judice lis est. Incunabula N.T. qui allegant, nonnisi conjecturis nituntur. Sane Cornelio Centurioni in baptismo vetus nomen haesit Act. X. uti prius Eunucho caloribus Aethiopicis infuscato Act. VIII ipsi etiam Saulo Act. IX. 18. coll. cum XI. 25. 30. XIII. 1. 7. 9. quo proximo loco primum Paulus appellatur, vel quia id nominis tanq. tropaeum subjugati Christo Sergii Pauli Proconsulis Cypri sibi ascivit, uti putat Hieron. vel quia a Sergio Paulo amicitiae gratia familiae suae nomine est nobilitatus, ut opinatur Crocius comm. in Ep. ad Ephes. p. 26. vel quia binomius fuit, ita ut nomini gentilitio Saulis, quod religionem & genus indicabat, ob summam φιλοτιμίαν additum fuerit Romanum illud Pauli, quod jus Romanae civitatis testaretur, ut praeeunte Origene judicant Calvin. comm. in Ep. ad Rom. c. 1. & Martyr comm. in 1. Cor. 1. Antiqua igitur adulti, qui ad Christianam religionem confluxerunt, plerunque retinuerunt nomina, quae quidem ante perceptum baptismum dare debuerunt, sed non ea fini, ut postmodum in baptismi administratione vel servarentur, vel immutarentur, verum ut nominetenus ad examen citarentur, ad baptismum praepararentur, & concinno ordine in tabulis collocarentur. Quod vero Dionysius Alexandrinus A.C. 260. juxta Alstedii calculum Chron. tit. 41. p. 401. Episcopus, comm. de promissionib. contra Nepotem Aegyptiorum Episcopum apud Eused. H.E. l. 7. c. 25. multos B. Johannis Apostoli temporibus, eo quod illum amarent, suspicerent, aemularentur, & in simili apud Deum pretio esse discuperent, Johannis nomen sibi usurpasse arbitratur, opinio est ex animo de autore Apocalypseos ambigente profecta. Morem enim Apostolorum appellationes arripiendi seculo II. nondum fuisse hinc colligunt Magdeburg. quia paucissimi ejus seculi Episcopi Apostoli cujusquam nomen referant, cent. 2. c. 6. p. 111, 112. Quicquid sit, ante aetatem Chrysostomi, qui circa A.C. 390. inclaruit, ὀνοματοθεσίαν baptismalem, praesertim in Ecclesia Orientali, non fuisse in usu, ex perverso quodam more, in cujus mentionem delabitur ille Christianorum Demosthenes hom. 12. in 1. Cor. etiam inter Christianos frequentato, quo infanti nomen imponituri accensis lucernis nomina assignabant, atque ejus demum, quae caeteris extinctis supervixerat, nomen puero indebant, hinc eum diuturnius victurum augurantes, optime conjectat Georg. Konig. caf. consc. Catech. p. 242. 243. Oppessulatus namque fuisset abusus iste, si propria infantibus nomina in baptismi collatione publica auctoritate fuissent impositia. Hinc quoque sudo clarius elucescit, eos qui sponsores, quorum rum originem sub Hygino Romano circa A.D.140. Episcopo ex Platina de vit. Pont. p. m. 17. ostendunt, nomina sua in susceptos transtulisse volunt, nihil habere quo se tueri possint.
units.tr: This exposition, as Laurentius on Paul, p. 440, thinks, is more learned and subtle than certain, or even very probable. For it is not clear how to be baptized for someone can mean the same as to receive someone's name in baptism. As to the time when Christians were first given names at the administration of baptism, the historians dispute, and the matter is still under judgement. Those who appeal to the infancy of the New Testament rely only on conjecture. To be sure, Cornelius the centurion kept his old name at baptism (Acts X); so did the Ethiopian eunuch, darkened by the Ethiopian heat (Acts VIII); and so did Saul himself (Acts IX. 18, compared with XI. 25, 30, XIII. 1, 7, 9), where he is first called Paul in the passage nearest to this. Either he took that name, as a trophy of his subjection to Christ, from Sergius Paulus the proconsul of Cyprus, as Jerome thinks; or he was made famous by his family name from Sergius Paulus, out of friendship, as Crocius, comm. in Ep. ad Ephes. p. 26, supposes; or he had two names, so that the Roman name Paul, which attested the right of Roman citizenship, was added to his family name Saul, which indicated his religion and his race, out of great love of honour [φιλοτιμία], as Calvin, comm. in Ep. ad Rom. c. 1, and Martyr, comm. in 1 Cor. 1, judge, following Origen. Adults who came to the Christian religion therefore generally kept the names they had, which they had to give before receiving baptism, but not for the purpose that they should be kept or changed in the administration of baptism afterwards. Rather they were called by name for examination, prepared for baptism, and entered in the registers in good order. As to what Dionysius of Alexandria, bishop, about A.D. 260 by Alsted's reckoning, Chron. tit. 41, p. 401, in his comm. de promissionibus contra Nepotem, a bishop of the Egyptians, reported by Eusebius, H.E. l. 7, c. 25, supposes, that in the time of the Apostle John many took the name of John for themselves, because they loved him, esteemed him, wished to rival him and to be held in like esteem before God, that opinion arises from a mind unsure about the author of the Apocalypse. For from this they conclude that the custom of the Apostles of taking names had not yet arisen in the second century, Magdeburg, because very few bishops of that century bear the name of any Apostle, cent. 2, c. 6, pp. 111, 112. Whatever the case, before the age of Chrysostom, who flourished about A.D. 390, the baptismal [ὀνοματοθεσία] name-giving was not in use, especially in the Eastern Church. Georg. König, caf. consc. Catech. pp. 242, 243, rightly conjectures this from a perverse custom, which the Christian Demosthenes hom. 12 in 1 Cor. mentions and which was also widely practised among Christians. When they were about to give a name to an infant, they lit lamps and assigned names to them; then the name of the lamp that had survived the others was given to the child, and from this they augured that he would live longer. For that abuse would have been forbidden if proper names had been imposed on infants at baptism by public authority. From this also it becomes all the clearer that those who want to transfer their own names to those they sponsor, whose origin they trace to the Roman bishop Hyginus about A.D. 140, Platina, de vit. Pont. p. m. 17, have nothing on which they can rely.

units.la: XXV. Sed navim avertentes ab istis argutiarum salebris velificationem dirigamus ad eos, qui locum nostrum Apostolicum non de speciali aliquo ritu, sed in genere de baptismo intelligunt, quem prisci temporibus ut plurimum immersione agi solitum arguit vel ipsa vocis tum Graecae βαπτίζειν immergere notantis, tum vernaculae Tauffen vel ab Heb. טבל immersit, vel a simpliciori Tief deductae proprietas. Cum autem immersio illa symbolum fuerit spiritualis mortificationis, qua caro submergitur & sepelitur, σημαντικώτερον Rom. VI. 3.4. ab hac Apostolum afferre argumentum nonnulli censent, in hunc sensum: Quid facient qui baptizantur ὡς νεκροί, tanquam mortui peccato & commortui Christo: vel pro mortuis (h.e. operibus peccati vita gratiae carentibus & mortem generantibus) abluendis? Frustra enim & temere in baptismo testamur, nos in mundo pro mortuis haberi & praesentis vitae voluptatibus nuntium mittere velle, si resurrectio non est futura. Laudantur in hanc sententiam Sedul. Primas. Haymo, Thomas, Contarenus: quibus ὁμοίως Vorstius tessarad. Antipist. par. 2. c. 12. sect. 11. p. 416. & Alting. Elenct. N. L. 20. p. 831. 832. Eadem immersio in aquam & mora sub aqua sicut illustris fuit typus & pictura mortis corporum, ita emersio ex aqua resurrectionis fuit τυπος, Rom. VI. 5. Hinc Chrysostomo hom. 40. in 1. Cor. baptizari pro mortuis est super professione articuli, οὐ πιστεύω εἰς νεκρῶν ἀνάστασιν, quem inter caeteros ex Symbolo recitabant Catechumeni, ad similitudinem mortuorum baptizari & demergi, dein sursum remeare & emergere. Ita Theodoreto comm. ad h.l. baptismus pro mortuis suscipitur, quod morientis ac resurgentis speciem quandam praefe ferat. Ex his exurgit hujuscemodi explicatus: Quid facient οἱ βαπτιζόμενοι ἐπ' ἐλπίδι τῆς ἀναστάσεως τῶν νεκρῶν, qui baptizantur in spem rei quam post mortem assecuturi sunt, videl. resurrectionis, cujus testera est baptismus. Suffragatores hujus explicationis citantur Oecumenius, Theophylactus, Photius: Hugo de S. Charo Cardin. & Glossa apud eundem, Cajetanus. Quibus suum addunt calculum P. Martyr comm. in 1. Cor. p. 418. Seb. Castalio annot. ad h.l. Polanus Syntag. Theol. T. II. l. 7. c. 25. qui tamen calculum reduxit Turr.Bab. p. 116.
units.tr: XXV. But turning our ship away from these rocks of subtle argument, let us steer our sail towards those who understand our Apostolic passage not of some special rite but in general of baptism. That baptism was for the most part performed in ancient times by immersion is shown both by the Greek word βαπτίζειν, meaning to immerse, and by the German word Tauffen, which comes from the Hebrew טבל [tabal], to dip, or from the plainer word Tief, deep. Since that immersion was a symbol of spiritual mortification, in which the flesh is submerged and buried, some think the Apostle draws his argument from this, in a more significant sense [σημαντικώτερον], Rom. VI. 3, 4, to this effect: What will those do who are baptized as dead men [ὡς νεκροί], as dead to sin and dead together with Christ? Or for the dead, that is, to wash away the works of sin, which lack the life of grace and bring forth death? For we vainly and rashly declare in baptism that we are regarded as dead in the world, and wish to send word to the pleasures of the present life, if there is no future resurrection. Sedulius, Primasius, Haymo, Thomas, Contarenus are cited for this view, and likewise Vorstius, Tessarad. Antichrist, part 2, c. 12, sect. 11, p. 416, and Alting, Elenct. N.L. 20, pp. 831, 832. The same immersion in the water and the stay under it, as it was a clear type and picture of the death of bodies, so the rising out of the water was the type [τύπος] of resurrection, Rom. VI. 5. Hence Chrysostom, hom. 40 in 1 Cor., says that to be baptized for the dead is, on the profession of the article I do not believe in the resurrection of the dead [οὐ πιστεύω εἰς νεκρῶν ἀνάστασιν], which the catechumens recited among the other articles of the Creed, to be baptized and plunged in the likeness of the dead, then to return upwards and rise again. So Theodoret in his commentary on this passage: baptism is received for the dead, because it bears a certain image of the dying and rising. From these points arises the following explanation: What will those do who are baptized in hope of the resurrection of the dead [ἐπ' ἐλπίδι τῆς ἀναστάσεως τῶν νεκρῶν], that is, who are baptized in hope of the thing they will obtain after death, namely the resurrection, of which baptism is the witness. The supporters of this explanation cited are Oecumenius, Theophylact, Photius, Hugh of St Cher the cardinal, and the Gloss on the same, Cajetan. To these they add their own opinion: P. Martyr, comm. in 1 Cor., p. 418; Sebastian Castellio, annot. ad h.l.; Polanus, Syntag. Theol. T. II, l. 7, c. 25, although he has reduced this opinion to Turrettin, Bab., p. 116.

units.la: XXVI. Verum & his expositionibus, cum extra aleam non sint, difficilius accedimus. Nam 1. Apostolum speciale quid attingere, nec de communi omnium baptismo, sed de quibusdam saltem baptizatis agere manifesta res docet, & personae mutatio evincit. Non enim unquam solet Apostolus de fidelibus in tertia persona loqui, cum de iis agit, quae fidelibus omnibus communia sunt, inquit Camerom yroth. Evang. p. 229. 2. Coacta est interpretatio phraseos, tum quia ὡς νεκροὶ & ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν, item baptizari pro mortuis & in baptismo repraesentare mortem ac resurrectionem seu baptizari in spem resurrectionis, sub idem significationis jugum devinciri nequeunt: tum quia articulus plane est incommodus: tum denique quia importuna ambiguitas suspensum redderet pium lectorem, si sub vocabulo νεκρῶν comprehenderentur peccata cum illud non nisi substantivo additum peccata notet, ut Heb. VI, 1. IX, 14. Conf. th. p. rat. 1. 3. Catechumeni quondam, quod ad Chrysost. sententiam observandum, non unum tantum Symboli articulum de resurrectione profitebantur, sed totum Symbolum. Quapropter si pro mortuis baptizari & in confessionem resurrectionis mortuorum baptizari eodem recidunt; pari ratione dici poterant pro Patre, Filio & Spiritu S. baptizari, quia in fidem de Patre, Filio & Spiritu S. baptizantur, quod tamen inusitatum.
units.tr: XXVI. But even these explanations are not beyond dispute, so we approach them with some hesitation. First, it is plainly evident, and the change of person proves, that the Apostle is touching on something special, and is speaking not of the common baptism of all, but at least of certain baptized persons. The Apostle never usually speaks of the faithful in the third person when he is dealing with things that are common to all the faithful, says Cameron, Camerom yroth. Evang. p. 229. Second, the interpretation of the phrase is forced. The expressions [ὡς νεκροὶ] and [ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν], as well as "to be baptized for the dead" and "in baptism to represent the death and resurrection," or "to be baptized in hope of the resurrection," cannot be yoked under the same yoke of meaning. Moreover, the article is plainly awkward. And finally, an unseasonable ambiguity would leave the pious reader in suspense if sins were understood under the word [νεκρῶν], since that word denotes sins only when it is added as a noun, as in Heb. 6:1 and 9:14. Conf. th. p. rat. 1. Third, catechumens once professed not just the one article of the Creed concerning the resurrection, but the whole Creed, as Chrysostom's view requires us to note. Therefore, if to be baptized for the dead and to be baptized into the confession of the resurrection of the dead come to the same thing, then by the same reasoning one could say "to be baptized for the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit," since they are baptized into faith in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. That usage, however, is unusual.

units.la: XXVII.
units.tr: XXVII.

units.la: Sic quoque in explicationibus ex Synecdochica sive Ecclesiastica verbi βαπτίζεσθαι acceptione promanantibus morati sumus: Metonymica, qua verbum istud prolotionibus generatim usurpatur, restat ut in deliberationem adducatur.
units.tr: In the same way we have dwelt on the explanations that arise from the synecdochical or ecclesiastical sense of the verb [βαπτίζεσθαι]. It remains to take up the metonymical sense, in which the word is used generally of ablutions.

units.la: XXVIII.
units.tr: XXVIII.

units.la: Nihil autem hic nominatius versione venerabilis Beza: Alioqui quid facient βαπτισμαῖς χρώμενοι ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν, qui ablutione utuntur super mortuis? Existimat nimirum ille, τὸ βαπτίζεσθαι significatione media notare ablutionem mortualem Gentilibus & Judaeis consuetam, qua mortuorum corpora in fidem & spem resurrectionis lavabantur. Haec opinio tulit puncta haud infimi subsellii virorum, Parei ad h.l. Chamieri Panstrat. Catholic. T. III. l. 26. c. 19. p. 1217. Crocii Anti-Becan. T. II. contr. 8. sect. 6. §. 25. p. 149. & Vvendelini Christ. Theol. l. 1. c. 27. p. m. 556. Germana huic, quam suggerit Bullingerus noster, Theologus veteranus, qui comm. in 1. Cor. p. 200, Apostolum Corinthiis objecisse putat Gentilium ceremoniam, quâ super mortua & sepulta corpora baptizabant, i.e. tingebant & aquam spargebant, sicque rigando aperte testabantur, flaccida ista in terram seminata corpora refloritura: ac proinde textum nostrum per enallagen legi posse censet: Si omnino non resurgent mortui, quid baptizant super mortuos?
units.tr: Nothing here is more explicit than the version of the venerable Beza: Otherwise, what will they do who make use of baptisms [βαπτισμαῖς χρώμενοι] for the dead, those who use ablution over the dead? He evidently thinks that [βαπτίζεσθαι], in the middle sense, denotes the ablution of the dead customary among Gentiles and Jews, by which the bodies of the dead were washed in faith and hope of the resurrection. This opinion has been held by men of no small standing: Parens on this passage, Chamier, Panstrat. Catholic. T. III, l. 26, c. 19, p. 1217; Crocius, Anti-Becan. T. II, contr. 8, sect. 6, §. 25, p. 149; and Wendelin, Christ. Theol. l. 1, c. 27, p. 556. Close to this is the view suggested by our Bullinger, an old theologian, who in his commentary on 1 Corinthians, p. 200, thinks that the Apostle was objecting to the Corinthians a Gentile ceremony by which they baptized, that is, sprinkled and poured water over, the dead and buried bodies, and by watering them openly bore witness that these limp bodies sown in the earth would bloom again. He therefore thinks our text may be read by enallage: If the dead rise not at all, why are they baptized over the dead?

units.la: XXIX. Subigit equidem fateri veritas, istum abluendi cadavera morem Apostoli aetate usurpari solitum fuisse partim à Gentilibus, apud quos mortui, membris ad naturalem corporis formam perductis, non aquâ tantum vivâ & purâ, sed admistis liquoribus odoratissimis aut floribus eliquatis lavabantur, & unguentis non vulgaribus ungebantur à pollinctoribus, ab ungenda pelle ita dictis, & à mulieribus, uti conjicitur ex illo Ennij: Tarquinij corpus bona femina lavit & unxit: partim ab ipsis Judaeis, ut indicium praebet locus Act. IX, 37. de Tabitha mortua: λούσαντες αὐτὴν ἔθηκαν ἐν ὑπερῴῳ, laverunt eam ac posuerunt in cænaculo: unde apud posteros eorum adhuc dum aquâ calidâ studiosè abluitur mortuus, ut purus & mundus sit, quum peccatorum ratio reddenda erit, teste in illorum scriptis exercitatissimo D. Buxtorsio synag. Iud. c. 35. p. m. 431. Neque etiam inficiamur, claram subinde lucem fulgetri instar sub obscura nocte coruscantis irradiasse Ethnicorum animos, cujus ductu mortem non interitum esse omnia delentem, sed quandam q. migrationem & vitae commutationem agnoverint, id quod ceremoniae eorum sepulchrales & summa in procurandis cadaveribus occupatio probabile efficiunt: hinc ille apud Ausonium, cui perpetuum ver agit iIlacrymabilis urna, commutavit secula, non obiit. Quia tamen τὸ βαπτίζεσθαι in significatione verbi medij de actione in aliud subjectum transeunte nullibi sumitur, & juxta illas interpretationes ὑπὲρ τῆς νεκρᾶς potius, quàm ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν dicendum fuisset, Apostoli dictum ad morem illum vel abluendi exanimes, vel (ut habet Ausonius) cineres mero spargendi, & odoro nardo, rosis puniceis, balsamóque perluendi referendum esse haud assentimur.
units.tr: XXIX. Truth indeed compels us to admit that this custom of washing corpses was in use in the Apostle's time, partly among the Gentiles, among whom the dead, once their limbs had been restored to their natural form, were washed not only with living and pure water but with water mixed with the most fragrant liquids or with melted flowers, and were anointed with uncommon ointments by undertakers (so called from anointing the skin) and by women, as may be conjectured from that line of Ennius: A good woman washed and anointed the body of Tarquin. Partly it was practised by the Jews themselves, as the passage about the dead Tabitha in Acts 9:37 indicates: [λούσαντες αὐτὴν ἔθηκαν ἐν ὑπερῴῳ] they washed her and laid her in an upper room. Hence even now among their descendants the dead are carefully washed with warm water, so that the dead man may be pure and clean when the reckoning of his sins is to be rendered, as the most learned Buxtorf, very well versed in their writings, testifies in Synag. Jud. c. 35, p. 431. Nor do we deny that at times a clear light, flashing like lightning through a dark night, has shone on the minds of the Gentiles, through whose guidance they recognised that death is not an annihilation that destroys all, but a certain migration and change of life. Their funeral ceremonies and their great care in preparing the corpses make this probable. Hence that line of Ausonius, for whom the tearless urn brings perpetual spring: He changed ages, he did not die. Yet since [τὸ βαπτίζεσθαι], as a middle verb denoting an action passing over to another subject, is nowhere used in this sense, and since on those interpretations one should rather have said [ὑπὲρ τῆς νεκρᾶς] than [ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν], we do not agree that the Apostle's words refer to that custom, whether of washing the lifeless or, as Ausonius has it, of sprinkling the ashes with wine and bathing them with fragrant nard, red roses and balsam.

units.la: XXX. Unica superest expositio, quae locum nostrum accipiendum dictitat de baptismo seu lotione ceremoniali Judaeorum, qui tangebant mortuos, quae praecipitur Num. XIX 11. & seqq. Qui tetigerit mortuum quodcunque cadaver hominis, is erit immundus septem diebs. Ubi autem purgaverit se aquâ separationis die tertio & die septimo, mundus erit: quòd si non purgabit se die tertio & die septimo, non erit mundus. Quisquis tacto mortuo, cadavere hominis qui mortuum est, non purgaverit se, tabernaculum Jehova polluit, ideò exscindetur anima illa ex Israële, quia aqua separationis non fuit aspersa super eum. Baptismum hunc eapropter à Deo per Mosen institutum, ut populus Israeliticus commonefieret resurrectionis mortuorum, qui autumant subiisse mentem Apostoli, verba ejus ita exponunt: Quid facient ij qui lavantur seu se lavant ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν, propter mortuos vel mortuorum gratiâ? Hunc sensum τῶν ἀμφοῖν amplectuntur approbatâ eruditione viri, Bonaventura Cornelius Bertramus, ὁμηλιξ Bezæ, lucubr. Franktall c.8.p.102.& seqq. Sebastianus Schmidt, Theologus Argentinensis, disp. Theol. de bapt. super mortuis th. 31. & seqq. qui ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν vertit super mortuis: & ἐλλογιμώτατος ille in Rep. Litt. heros, ὁ ἐν μαχαιρίτης Hottingerus noster, Præceptor nunquam sine elogio dicendus, dissert. de variis Orientis inscriptionib. & mensuris, præmissa cippis Hebr. p.10.11.
units.tr: XXX. One explanation alone remains, which insists that our passage must be taken of the baptism, or ceremonial washing, of the Jews who touched the dead, as commanded in Num. 19:11 and following: He that toucheth the dead body of any man shall be unclean seven days. But if he purify himself with the water of separation on the third day, and on the seventh day, he shall be clean; but if he purify not himself the third day, and the seventh day, he shall not be clean. Whosoever toucheth the dead, the body of a man that is dead, and purifieth not himself, defileth the tabernacle of the LORD; and that soul shall be cut off from Israel: because the water of separation was not sprinkled upon him, he shall be unclean. Those who think the mind of the Apostle went this way therefore hold that this baptism was instituted by God through Moses so that the people of Israel might be reminded of the resurrection of the dead, and they explain his words thus: What shall they do who are washed, or who wash themselves [ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν], on account of the dead, or for the sake of the dead? This sense is embraced by men of approved learning: Bonaventura Cornelius Bertram, Beza's contemporary (lucubr. Franktall c. 8, p. 102 and following); Sebastian Schmidt, theologian of Strasbourg (disp. Theol. de bapt. super mortuis, th. 31 and following), who renders [ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν] as "over the dead"; and that most illustrious hero of the Republic of Letters, our Hottinger [ὁ ἐν μαχαιρίτης], who must always be spoken of with praise, in his dissertation on the various inscriptions and measures of the East, prefixed to the Hebrew cippi, p. 10, 11.

units.la: XXXI.
units.tr: XXXI.

units.la: Equidem, utrum cadat explicatio isthæc, an rectò stet talo, Candidi Lectoris judicio permissum esto. Nos sanè illam, monitu instructúque Clarissimi ac Reverendi Dn. Præsidis edocti, & nube examinatarum opinionum, quarum singulæ non unâ laborant difficultate, detersâ oculos aperientes, τὰ πρωτεῖα obtinere, genuinámque esse & αὐτόφυη asserere non veremur. Ut autem sententiæ nostræ fides abundantior sit, nei neque phraseologiam, neque modum argumentandi Apostolicum adversari demonstratum ibimus.
units.tr: Whether this explanation stands or falls, I leave to the judgement of the candid reader. For my part, instructed and guided by the counsel of the most distinguished and reverend Lord President, and having wiped away the cloud of opinions that we have examined (each of which labours under more than one difficulty), we do not hesitate to claim the first place [τὰ πρωτεῖα] for it, opening our eyes, and to assert that it is genuine and native [αὐτόφυη]. So that confidence in our view may be the stronger, we shall go on to show that it is opposed neither to the phraseology nor to the manner of arguing of the Apostle.

units.la: XXXII.
units.tr: XXXII.

units.la: Circa phraseologiam singulorum vocabulorum pondus seriâ mentis indagine expendendum occurrit. Ἐπεὶ τί ποιήσουσιν οἱ βαπτιζόμενοι ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν; inquit Apostolus. Particulam ἐπεὶ appositè per præterea cum Grotio, vel cum plerisque aliis per ἐπεὶ μὴ, alioqui vertere possumus, quippe quæ, veluti transitionis nota, novum pro resurrectione argumentum ab absurdo consequenti petitum in medium poni indicat. Vocula τί, Apostolum bonitate causæ suæ fretum ipsos Corinthios, ut testimonium eorum extorqueat, in consilium adhibere sententiámque rogare, nobis demonstrat. Persona tertia ποιήσουσιν & articulus distinctivus οἱ verbo βαπτιζόμενοι appositus ritum non universalem & ubique receptum, sed particularem & aliquibus saltem, putà Judæis etiam conversis, usitatum indigitat. Se ipsum tamen, utpote Judæum natione, non inclusit Apostolus, vel quia Gentiles infirmiores offendere religioni habuit, vel quia inter gentes, cùm factus fuerit τοῖς πᾶσι τὰ πάντα 1. Cor. IX. 22. isto ritu Judaico non fuit usus. Verbum βαπτίζεσθαι lavari nobis & ablutionibus expurgari designat. Derivatur enim à βάπτειν, quod est lanam aut aliud quidvis immersum in lacum aliquem aquâ tinctoriâ plenum inficere & colorare, indeque βαπτίζειν proprie tingendi causâ est immergere: Quia verò quæ ex aquis emerguntur lota apparent & munda, idcirco ex consequenti βαπτίζειν notat immunditias loto etiam toto corpore emaculare & munditiem in earum locum inducere: hinc βαπτισμοὶ in N.T. frequenter καθαρισμὸς seu ablutiones, easque vel legales seu Leviticas, quarum meminit autor Epistolæ ad Hebræos (quam Paulo, non Barnabæ, non Lucæ, non Marco, non Clementi Rom. non denique alii transscribimus) c. IX. v. 10. vel superstitiosas seu Pharisaicas, ut Marc. VII. 4. 8. significant. Est verò τὸ βαπτίζεσθαι hujuscemodi passivum, per quod passio reflectitur seu reciprocatur in ipsum agentem, adeóque reddi potest lavare, abluere se ipsum. Cui versioni infignitius favet locus Marc. VII. 4. de Pharisæis: Καὶ ἀπὸ ἀγορᾶς, ἐὰν μὴ βαπτίσωνται, οὐκ ἐσθίουσι, & à foro (sub. ὅταν ἔλθωσι, quum venerint) nisi se abluant, non edunt: Cùm enim Pharisæi βαπτιζόμενοι è publico tanq. à contagione & pollutione עם האיש vel עם הארץ vulgi redirent, totum corpus lavabant, qua de re videri poterit Drusius comm. de trib. sect. Iud. l. 2. p. 97. Consimilis est usus verbi νίπτεσθαι l. c. v. 3. Pharisæi & omnes Iudæi, ἐὰν μὴ πυγμῇ νίψωνται τὰς χεῖρας, non edunt, ubi phrasis πυγμὴ νίπτεσθαι aliis idem est quod πύκτα seu πυκνῶς frequenter; aliis sedulò ac diligenter, certatim, iterum atque iterum, metaphorâ à πυγμῇ h. e. pugna pugilum, qui iteratis pugnis decertando ad palmam contendebant, deducta, unde πυγμὴ πλίειν est crebrò ferire; aliis idem quod באגרף πυγμῇ pugno in cavum manus alterius immisso defricare sordes; aliis denique נטילת ידיים χειραφρίαν seu elevationem manuum in pugni figuram compositarum notat, quâ Judæi manuum lotioni operam daturi quinque digitorum ἄκρα inter se jungunt, de qua χειρολαβία nos instruit Dictator ille Reip. Litt. Iof. Scaliger Elench. Trihæres. c. 7. Ita Jacobus Patriarcha, Sichemitidas fœmellas, aliósque, qui jam apud eum versati sunt, Ethnicos in familiam Ecclesiámque suam cooptaturus Gen. XXXV. 2. והטהרו & mundami-ni, ni, inquit, h. e. mundate seu lavate vos: quo in loco originem Baptismi Proselytici טבילת גרות dicti, qui traductio fuit Gentilium in religionem Judaicam, ostendit Lightfootus Hor. Hebr. in Matth. III. 6. Et haec ipsa τὸ βαπτίζεσθαι actionem notare reciprocam satis superque confirmant. Sequitur ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν, quod jam interpretati sumus propter mortuos vel mortuorum causa. In hoc significatu saepissime sumi praepositionem ὑπὲρ cum secundo casu constructam satis obvium est Rom. I. v. 5. XV. v. 8, 9. 2. Cor. I. v. 6. Eph. III. v. 13. Phil. I. v. 29. II. 13. Col. I. v. 24. 2. Thess. I. 5. II. 1. aliisque locis. Ita νεκρὸς maximè proprie sonare mortuos homines, tam apertum est ut nihil aliud magis. Articulus τῶν, cujus ut absentia ἀόριστος, ita adjectio, ex Scaligeri effato, ἐμφατικὴ est ἡ ὀρισμένη, vocabulo νεκρῶν limites ponit, ut comprehendat τὰς ζῶντας νεκρὰς, certos mortuos, illos nempe, qui tanguntur & propter quos tangentes abluuntur. Denique a phrasi βαπτίζεσθαι ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν haud abludit illa Siracid. XXXIV. 29. baptizari ἀπὸ τῆς νεκρῶς, a cadavere seu post tactum cadaver se lavare.
units.tr: Regarding the phraseology, the weight of each individual word has to be weighed by careful mental inquiry. Otherwise, what will those who are baptized for the dead do? [Ἐπεὶ τί ποιήσουσιν οἱ βαπτιζόμενοι ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν;] says the Apostle. The particle ἐπεὶ we may fittingly render as moreover, with Grotius, or, with most others, as otherwise [ἐπεὶ μὴ], since it, as a mark of transition, indicates that a new argument for the resurrection, drawn from an absurd consequence, is brought forward. The little word τί [what] shows us that the Apostle, relying on the goodness of his cause, calls the Corinthians themselves into counsel, asks their opinion, and so wrings from them their testimony. The third person ποιήσουσιν [will do] and the distinctive article οἱ placed before the verb βαπτιζόμενοι [being baptized] point to a rite that is not universal and received everywhere, but particular and in use among some only, for instance among Jews, even converted ones. Yet the Apostle did not include himself, although a Jew by birth, either because he thought it wrong to offend the weaker Gentiles, or because, among the Gentiles, since he had become all things to all men [τοῖς πᾶσι τὰ πάντα], 1. Cor. IX. 22., he did not use this Jewish rite. The verb βαπτίζεσθαι [baptizesthai] signifies, for us, to be washed and cleansed by ablutions. For it derives from βάπτειν [baptein], which means to dye and colour wool or any other thing dipped into some pool full of dye-water; and so βαπτίζειν [baptizein] properly means to immerse for the sake of dyeing. But since things that come up out of the water appear washed and clean, βαπτίζειν consequently means to wash away uncleanness, even by bathing the whole body, and to bring cleanness in its place. Hence in the New Testament βαπτισμοί [baptismoi] frequently mean καθαρισμός [katharismos], that is, ablutions, and these either legal or Levitical, of which the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews speaks (which we ascribe to Paul, not to Barnabas, nor Luke, nor Mark, nor Clement of Rome, nor indeed to anyone else), c. IX. v. 10., or superstitious or Pharisaic, as in Mark VII. 4. 8. Now τὸ βαπτίζεσθαι [to baptizesthai] is a passive of this kind, by which the action is reflected or returns upon the agent himself, and so it can be rendered to wash, to cleanse oneself. This rendering is strongly supported by Mark VII. 4 about the Pharisees: And when they come from the market, unless they wash themselves, they do not eat [Καὶ ἀπὸ ἀγορᾶς, ἐὰν μὴ βαπτίσωνται, οὐκ ἐσθίουσι]; and from the market (understood: when they have come) unless they wash themselves, they do not eat. For when the Pharisees, being baptized [βαπτιζόμενοι], returned from the public place, as from contact with and pollution by the common people, am ha-ish [עם האיש] or am ha-aretz [עם הארץ], they washed the whole body. On this matter, see Drusius, Commentary on the Three Jewish Sects, book 2, p. 97. The use of the verb νίπτεσθαι [niptesthai] in the same passage, v. 3, is similar: The Pharisees and all the Jews, unless they wash their hands with the fist [Pharisæi & omnes Iudæi, ἐὰν μὴ πυγμῇ νίψωνται τὰς χεῖρας] do not eat, where the phrase πυγμὴ νίπτεσθαι [pygmē niptesthai] means to some the same as πύκτα or πυκνῶς [pykta or pyknōs], that is, often; to others, diligently and carefully, eagerly, again and again, a metaphor drawn from πυγμῇ [pygmē], the fighting of boxers, who by repeated blows strove for the palm, whence πυγμὴ πλίειν [pygmē pleiein] is to strike often; to others it is the same as be-egroph [באגרף], rubbing off the dirt by pressing the fist into the hollow of the other hand; and finally, to others it denotes netilath yadayim [נטילת ידיים], the washing of hands, χειραφρίαν [cheirafrian], or the raising of the hands formed into the shape of a fist, by which the Jews, about to wash their hands, join the tips of the five fingers together; of this χειρολαβία [cheirolabia] we are informed by that famous dictator of the republic of letters, Joseph Scaliger, Elenchus Trihaeresii, c. 7. So Jacob the patriarch, about to admit into his household and church the Shechemite women and others, Gentiles who had already been living with him, says, and be clean [והטהרו], Gen. XXXV. 2.: cleanse yourselves, that is, wash yourselves. In that place Lightfoot, Hebrew Horae on Matthew III. 6., shows the origin of the so-called baptism of proselytes, tevilath gerut [טבילת גרות], which was the passing of Gentiles into the Jewish religion. These very instances sufficiently and more than sufficiently confirm that τὸ βαπτίζεσθαι signifies a reflexive action. There follows ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν [hyper tōn nekrōn], which we have already rendered for the dead or for the sake of the dead. That the preposition ὑπὲρ [hyper], construed with the genitive, is very often taken in this sense is clear enough from Rom. I. v. 5., XV. v. 8, 9., 2. Cor. I. v. 6., Eph. III. v. 13., Phil. I. v. 29., II. 13., Col. I. v. 24., 2. Thess. I. 5., II. 1., and other places. That νεκρός [nekros] most properly means dead men is as plain as anything could be. The article τῶν [tōn], whose absence makes it indefinite (ἀόριστος) and whose addition, by Scaliger's saying, makes the definite article emphatic (ἐμφατικὴ ἡ ὀρισμένη), sets limits to the word νεκρῶν, so that it takes in certain dead, namely those who are touched and on whose account the touchers are washed. Finally, the phrase βαπτίζεσθαι ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν [baptizesthai hyper tōn nekrōn] is not far from that in Sirach XXXIV. 29.: to be washed from the dead body [baptizari ἀπὸ τῆς νεκρῶς], that is, to wash oneself from a corpse, or after touching a corpse.

units.la: XXXIII.
units.tr: XXXIII.

units.la: Sicut autem versio nostra phraseologiae, ita modo etiam argumentandi Apostolico quàm optimè congruit. Eò namque collineat Apostolus, ut resurrectionem mortuorum ab exemplis toto quasi orbe conspicuis confirmet. Horsum merito refert tam laboriosos lotionum Judaicarum apparatus, qui Israelitis recordationem resurrectionis dare debuerunt. Cùm enim demortui homines tumulari nequiverint, quin eorum cadavera contingerentur; cura verò corporum sepulchris afficiendorum, ut ipsa sepulchrorum religio, momentosum speratae resurrectionis corporum argumentum perhibeatur & monimentum: convenienter Apostolum ex lotionibus Judaeorum propter mortuos ad officium sepulturae iteratis argumentum repetiisse censet Bertramus lucubr. Franktall. c. 8. p. 103. qui textum nostrum istâ paraphrasi opportunè illustravit: Praeterea si nulla est spes resurrectionis, quorsum Hebraei nostri ex antiquissimo aeterni Dei mandato cum tanta tamque exquisita sedulitate mortuorum sepulturam procurant? itaut se repetitis per aliquot dies ablutionibus fatigare non dubitent, quibus expurgent pollutiones, quas ex humatis corporibus mortuorum contraxerunt. Quin potiùs illi qui etiamnum hodie sese & alios sepeliendis mortuorum corporibus miris modis fatigant, curam illam tam piam; & sanctâ deinceps missam facient, neq; amplius mortuorum corpora contingere sustinebunt, imò nec contingendis in posterum mortuorum corporibus sese polluere volent, postq. nullum percipient levamentum laborum illorum, quos sepeliendis mortuorum corporibus impendunt: neque ullum lotionum illarum quas ipsi aliíque in eorum gra-tiam ingeminant, ut pollutiones contractas ex contactu inter sepeliendum mortuorum corporibus eluant, operaque sua tam accurata aquamentum vel certè solatium situm in resurrectionis corporum demortuorum spe & fide, quam jam inde ab Orbis conditu omnes fere gentes in cura sepeliendis mortuis adhibita testata sunt & adumbrârunt. Hæc Bertramus, in cujus sententiam pedibus imus. Sed & ille ipse baptismus legalis, quo (prout prolixiori tractu orationis describitur Num. XIX.) mortui attactu inquinati aquâ lustrationis cinere junicis rufæ extra castra combustæ condita & instar lixivii colatâ purgandi fuerût, & sine quo ad res sacras admitti non potuerût, fuit veluti reditus à morte ad vitam. Nam pollutio legalis per contactum cadaveris significabat lege communé peccati & mortis: unde pollutus talis & legaliter non purificatus exscindendus dicitur ex Israële Num. XIX.13. Ablutio autem illa ceremonialis, ceu medium redeundi à morte ad vitam, typus erat resurrectionis, quam meditari necesse habuit populus Israeliticus. Hinc optimo jure argumentū pro resurrectione tale petit Apostolus: Si non est resurrectio, frustra quidam Βαπτιζονται υπερ των νεκρων, cum eo baptismo obsignantes spem resurrectionis: imò frustra Deus ritum illum molestum instituit, quod dicere non tantùm absurdum, sed & impium.
units.tr: Just as our version fits the Apostle's phraseology, so his mode of argument agrees very well with it. For the Apostle aims to confirm the resurrection of the dead from examples visible, as it were, throughout the whole world. To this purpose rightly belong the laborious Jewish washings, which were meant to give the Israelites a reminder of the resurrection. For since dead men could not be buried without their corpses being touched, and since the care taken in preparing bodies for the grave is held to be a weighty argument for, and a reminder of, the hoped-for resurrection of bodies, just as the very reverence shown to tombs is, Bertram of Frankenthal (Lucubr. Franktall. c. 8, p. 103) fittingly judges that the Apostle drew his argument from the Jewish washings repeated for the dead after the duty of burial. He illustrated our text aptly with this paraphrase: Furthermore, if there is no hope of resurrection, why do our Hebrews, by the most ancient command of the eternal God, procure the burial of the dead with such great and exact diligence, that they do not hesitate to weary themselves with washings repeated over several days, by which they cleanse the pollutions they contracted from the buried bodies of the dead? Rather, those who even today wear themselves and others out in marvellous ways in burying the bodies of the dead will abandon that so pious care, and will henceforth regard it as sacred no longer; nor will they any more endure to touch the bodies of the dead, nor will they wish to defile themselves by touching such bodies in future, since they will perceive no relief from those labours which they expend in burying the bodies of the dead, nor from any of those washings which they and others repeat on their behalf, to cleanse the pollutions contracted from contact in burying the dead bodies; and since their work so carefully done would yield no water, or at least no solace, founded on the hope and faith in the resurrection of the bodies of the dead, which almost all nations, from the beginning of the world, have attested and foreshadowed in the care they have given to burying the dead. Thus Bertram; and we follow his opinion wholeheartedly. But that legal baptism too, by which (as is described at greater length in Num. XIX) those defiled by touching a dead body were to be cleansed with water of lustration, prepared from the ashes of a red heifer burnt outside the camp and strained like lye, and without which they could not be admitted to holy things, was a kind of return from death to life. For legal pollution through contact with a corpse signified the common law of sin and death; hence one who was polluted and not legally purified is said to be to be cut off from Israel (Num. XIX.13). That ceremonial washing, however, as a means of returning from death to life, was a type of the resurrection, which the people of Israel were bound to meditate upon. Hence the Apostle very rightly takes his argument for the resurrection in this form: If there is no resurrection, why are some baptized for the dead [Βαπτίζονται ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν], sealing with that baptism their hope of resurrection? Indeed, God would in vain have instituted that troublesome rite, which is not only absurd but even impious to say.

units.la: XXXIV. Quorsum verò, inquias, Apostolus ista ex lege Mo- saica ad Corinthiorum, ceu Gentilium, errores explodendos eruit?
units.tr: XXXIV. But why, you will ask, does the Apostle bring these things out of the Mosaic law to refute the errors of the Corinthians, who were Gentiles?

units.la: Resp. 1. Corinthum, Achajæ caput, aliuisse Judæos, quorum bene multi Christo nomen dederint, ex Act. XVIII.2.4.8.& 1.Cor.I.14. liquidò patescit. Illos autem, ut familiarius se cum Judæis aliis, qui in ceremoniis Judaicis toti adhuc hærebant, conjungerent, eósque Christo lucrifacerent, ad horum mores sese attemperâsse, testis locuples est locus Act. XXI.20. Vides frater quot myriades sint Iudæorum qui crediderunt, & omnes amulatores sunt legis. Alioquin Judæis Ecclesiæ filiis, ipsi etiam Paulo vel Barnabæ, in Synagogas Judæorum nondum conversorum intrare non fuisset integrum, nisi purificationum Mosaicarum aliquam habuissent rationem. Actum igitur Apostolus suo adhuc tempo-re re in Ecclesia vigentem Corinthiis diligenti æstimatione perpendendum sistit. 2. Allusiones & argumentationes ex legis Mosaicæ ceremoniis plurimas expromit S. Apostolus tum in reliquis suis Epistolis, tum in hac ipsa: vid. 1 Cor. V. 7. 8. IX. 8. 1 3. X. 2. 1 8. Ita v. 20. cap. nostri XV. Christus dicitur ἀπαρχὴ τῶν κεκοιμημένων, primitia eorum qui obdormiverunt, similitudine a primitiis in V. T. oblatis desumptâ, quam erudite explanat Clariss. Dn. Hoffmeist. Panac. p. 147. 148. 3. Quoniam Apostoli argumentum nititur autoritate ipsius Dei, qui baptismum illum ceremonialem, ut esset resurrectionis mortuorum commonitorium, sanxit, levi apud Corinthios pendere momento neutiquam potuit. Stat igitur expositio nostra: Quid facient qui se lavant propter mortuos? nec vel phraseologiæ, vel modo argumentandi Apostolico quicquam adversatur, ὅπερ ἐδλει δξιξαι.
units.tr: Answer. 1. That Corinth, the capital of Achaia, had Jews, of whom a good many had given their name to Christ, is clear from Acts XVIII.2, 4, 8, and 1 Cor. I.14. That these Corinthians, in order to associate more familiarly with the other Jews, who still clung wholly to the Jewish ceremonies, and so to win them to Christ, had accommodated themselves to their customs, is sufficiently shown by Acts XXI.20: You see, brother, how many myriads of Jews there are who have believed, and they are all zealous for the law. Otherwise it would not have been lawful for Jewish sons of the Church, and even for Paul or Barnabas, to enter the synagogues of the Jews who were not yet converted, unless they had some regard for the Mosaic purifications. The Apostle therefore sets before the Corinthians a custom still in force in the Church of his own time, to be weighed with careful judgement. 2. The holy Apostle brings forward very many allusions to and arguments from the ceremonies of the Mosaic law, both in his other Epistles and in this one itself: see 1 Cor. V.7, 8; IX.8, 13; X.2, 18. So at v. 20 of our chapter XV, Christ is called the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep [ἀπαρχὴ τῶν κεκοιμημένων], a comparison drawn from the firstfruits offered in the Old Testament, which the most distinguished Mr. Hoffmeister learnedly explains (Panac. pp. 147, 148, 3). Since the Apostle's argument rests on the authority of God himself, who instituted that ceremonial baptism so that it might be a reminder of the resurrection of the dead, it could by no means have been of little weight among the Corinthians. Our exposition therefore stands: What will they do who are washed for the dead? and nothing in the Apostle's phraseology or mode of argument is opposed to it, which was to be shown [ὅπερ ἔδει δεῖξαι].

units.la: Primitiæ messis faciunt spem divitis, atque Qua fructus produnt sit bonitate sequens. Primitiæ ingenii, quid sit de messe tenendum Doctrinæ, erudiunt dexteritate sua. Ingenii quas tu profers Cognate diserte Primitias, laudem non mereantur eæ? Quidni? Nam messem promittunt (spero) refertam Doctrinæ pulchris frugibus atque bonis. Eja cole ingenii proporro fideliter agrum, Et quo coepisti currere perge pede. Namque tibi largam messem cumulabis honorum Aoniis studiis invigilando probè. Ut decus esse queas patriæ spésque ampla tuorum Concedat summi gratia summa Dei.
units.tr: The first-fruits of the harvest give hope of a rich yield, and by their goodness they reveal the quality of the crop that follows. The first-fruits of your talent teach, by their skill, what we may expect from the harvest of learning. Cousin, do the first-fruits of talent that you eloquently present not deserve praise? Why not? For they promise, I hope, a harvest crammed with the fair and good fruits of learning. Come, go on faithfully cultivating the field of your talent, and press on with the foot with which you began to run. For you will heap up for yourself a generous harvest of honours by watching diligently over the Aonian studies, so that you may be an ornament to your homeland and a great hope to your kin, by the highest grace of the highest God.

units.la: II. Felix est animi Dædala quem suis ditavit variis dotibus ingeni, donavitque Minerva sanæ mentis acumine. Felix ille virûm dicitur omnium, quem Musæ gremio suscipiunt suo Diuæ, quemve fovent in sincero quoque pectore. Fausus terque quater, dicier ampliùs & si quid poterit, Tuque merebere, Nam Te Pallas amica lymphis Aoniis rigat. Finxit Te manibus Clio suis sacra Instruxit(nec enim prospicit omnib.) ac Tritonia virgo claris dotibus ingeni. Ergo Tu vigilans, ut potes,excole nec vires animi neglige, sedulus Musùm castra secutus, exhauri latices sacros. Donec Castalidum cantet adoream Coetus, maneant sertáque laurea Te perchare profundam non visura caliginem.
units.tr: II. Happy is the man whom skilful Daedalus has enriched with various gifts of mind, and whom Minerva has endowed with the keenness of a sound understanding. Happy above all men, they say, is he whom the divine Muses take into their lap, or cherish in their sincere heart. Thrice and four times blessed you will be called, and whatever more can be said, and you deserve it; for Pallas, your friend, waters you with Aonian streams. Clio shaped you with her own hands and equipped you with sacred gifts (for she does not look upon everyone), and the Tritonian virgin with the bright gifts of talent. So, watchful as you are, cultivate your powers and do not neglect the strength of your mind; diligently following the camps of the Muses, drink deep of the sacred streams, until the company of the Castalides sings your praise, and laurel wreaths remain for you, dear one, who will never see the deep darkness.

units.la: III. Falleris Ausoni Præsul, qui dogma nefandum, Purgantem hinc ignem, cudere ritè cupis. Purpureo CHRISTI jam sunt qui sanguine loti, Sulphureo tristi, non opus,igne luant. Si tu, síque tui Stygiis immergier undis Mavultis, per me, crede, manere licet. Interea, Cognate,loci te vindice sensus Quòd patet, hinc laus est certa reposta tibi.
units.tr: III. You are mistaken, Ausonian prelate, if you are eager to forge here the impious dogma of a purifying fire. Those already washed in the purple blood of Christ have no need to pay the penalty in the gloomy sulphurous fire. If you and yours prefer to be plunged into the Stygian waves, believe me, you may remain there. Meanwhile, cousin, the sense of the passage, as it lies open, vindicates you, and so a sure praise is laid up for you.
